name: Aloo Baingan

ingredients.prep: cut into 1-inch cubes and kept in salted water

steps: Cut the brinjal into 1-inch cubes and drop them straight into a bowl of salted water so they do not darken. Peel the potato and cut it into 3/4-inch cubes, slightly smaller than the brinjal, since it takes longer to cook.
Heat the oil in a kadhai on medium (if using mustard oil, let it just smoke first, then lower the heat). Add the cumin seeds and hing and let them crackle.
Add the onion and saute 5-6 minutes until golden. Add the ginger, garlic and green chilli and saute 1 minute.
Add the turmeric, red chilli powder and coriander powder, stir for 20 seconds, then add the tomato and salt. Cook 4-5 minutes until the tomato is soft and oil shows at the edges.
Add the potato and stir to coat. Cover and cook on low for 7-8 minutes, stirring once, sprinkling in a splash of water if it sticks.

Drain the brinjal and add it to the pan. Stir gently, cover and cook on low for another 10-12 minutes, stirring gently every 4 minutes, until the brinjal is soft and a potato cube breaks easily when pressed.
Uncover, sprinkle the amchur and garam masala, fold gently and cook 1-2 minutes more. Scatter the coriander leaves and serve.
tips: Always give the potato a head start: if both go in together, the brinjal collapses into mush before the potato is cooked.
Use firm, glossy brinjals with a fresh green cap that spring back when pressed; dull, wrinkled or soft ones are old, seedy and more bitter.
Stir with a gentle folding motion once the brinjal is in so the pieces stay whole.

name: Aloo Gobi

ingredients.prep: cut into 1.5-inch florets, washed in warm salted water and patted dry

steps: Cut the cauliflower into florets and the potato into cubes a little smaller than the florets, so both finish cooking together. Dry the washed florets well.
Heat the oil in a wide heavy kadai on medium heat. Add the cumin seeds and let them splutter for 20-30 seconds.
Add the onion and saute for 3-4 minutes until soft and lightly golden. Add the ginger and green chilli and stir for 30 seconds.

Turn the heat to low, add the turmeric, red chilli powder and coriander powder and stir for 15-20 seconds. Add the tomato and cook for 3-4 minutes, mashing with the spatula, until soft and the oil starts to show at the edges.
Add the potato, stir to coat in the masala and cook on medium for 2 minutes. Add the cauliflower and salt and toss gently until every piece is coated.
Cover and cook on low heat for 15-18 minutes without adding water, turning gently with a flat spatula every 4-5 minutes. If it starts to catch at the bottom, sprinkle 1-2 tablespoons of water only.
Check that a knife goes through the potato easily. Uncover, raise the heat to medium and cook 3-4 minutes, turning gently, until any moisture dries off and the edges brown lightly.
Sprinkle over the garam masala and amchur, toss for a minute, turn off the heat and finish with the coriander leaves.
tips: Do not add water: the covered pan steams the vegetables in their own moisture, and water turns the cauliflower mushy.
Stir by lifting and folding from the bottom with a flat spatula; vigorous stirring breaks the florets.
Cut the potato smaller than the cauliflower, otherwise the cauliflower is overcooked by the time the potato is done.

name: Aloo Matar

ingredients.prep: shelled fresh peas or frozen peas (buy about double this weight in the pod)

steps: Heat the oil in a pressure cooker on medium heat. Add the cumin seeds and asafoetida; when the cumin sizzles, add the onion and fry for 5-6 minutes until golden.
Add the ginger and green chilli and saute for 30 seconds. Add the tomato and cook for 2 minutes until it starts to soften.
Add the turmeric powder, kashmiri red chilli powder, coriander powder and salt. Cook for 4-5 minutes, stirring, until the tomato breaks down completely and oil separates.
Add the potato and fresh peas and stir for 2 minutes to coat them in the masala.
Pour in the water, stir, close the lid and pressure-cook on medium heat for 2 whistles (about 8-10 minutes). Let the pressure release on its own.
Open the cooker and lightly mash a few potato pieces against the side with the ladle to thicken the gravy. Add the garam masala and simmer uncovered for 2-3 minutes; add hot water if it is too thick.
Garnish with coriander leaves and serve hot.
tips: Mashing a few potato cubes into the gravy is what gives home-style aloo matar its body; no cream or cashew is needed.
If you are using frozen peas, add them after pressure cooking and simmer for 4-5 minutes, or they turn mushy.
The gravy thickens as it stands, so keep it slightly thinner than you want when you switch off.

name: Sukhi Aloo Matar
steps: Rinse the potato cubes and drain them well. Shell the peas if using fresh.
Heat the oil in a kadai on medium heat. Add the cumin seeds and let them splutter for 20-30 seconds.
Add the onion and saute for 4-5 minutes until light golden. Add the ginger and green chilli and stir for 30 seconds.

Turn the heat to low, add the turmeric, red chilli powder and coriander powder and stir for 15-20 seconds. Add the tomato with a pinch of the salt and cook for 3-4 minutes until soft and pulpy and the oil starts to separate.
Add the potato and the rest of the salt and stir for 2 minutes on medium heat. If using fresh peas, add them now.

Sprinkle 2-3 tablespoons of water, cover and cook on low heat for 12-15 minutes, stirring every 4-5 minutes, until the potato is tender all the way through. If using frozen peas, stir them in for the last 5 minutes.
Uncover and cook on medium heat for 2-3 minutes, stirring, until the sabzi is dry and the masala clings to the potatoes.
Sprinkle the garam masala and amchur, toss well and finish with the coriander leaves.
tips: Keep the potato cubes small and even; big chunks stay raw inside while the masala scorches.
Frozen peas go in only at the end, otherwise they turn wrinkled and grey.
Use just a splash of water to steam; this is a dry sabzi, so it should end with no liquid in the pan.

name: Aloo Palak

ingredients.prep: washed well, drained and roughly chopped

steps: Wash the spinach in 2-3 changes of water until no grit settles at the bottom, drain well in a colander and chop roughly; thin tender stems can go in. Peel the potatoes and cut them into 3/4-inch cubes.

Heat the oil in a kadhai on medium (if using mustard oil, let it just smoke first, then lower the heat). Add the cumin seeds and hing and let them crackle. Add the onion and saute 4-5 minutes until light golden.
Add the garlic, ginger and green chilli and saute 1 minute until the garlic smells cooked.

Add the potatoes, turmeric, red chilli powder, coriander powder and a little salt, and stir for 2 minutes to coat. Cover and cook on low for 10-12 minutes, stirring every 3-4 minutes, until a knife goes into a potato with just slight resistance. Sprinkle a splash of water if they stick.
Uncover, raise the heat to medium-high and add the spinach a handful at a time, stirring each lot in until it wilts, about 2 minutes in all.
Keep cooking uncovered on medium-high for 5-7 minutes, stirring often, until the water the spinach releases has evaporated, the potatoes are fully tender and the spinach clings to them.
Stir in the garam masala, taste for salt, cook 1 more minute and serve hot.
tips: Salt lightly at first: the spinach shrinks to a fraction of its volume and the dish can easily end up too salty.
Keep the pan uncovered once the spinach goes in; covering it turns the leaves dull olive and leaves the sabzi watery.
Cook the potatoes almost done before adding spinach, or the spinach overcooks while you wait for them.

name: Aloo Paratha

ingredients.prep: boiled in the skin, peeled and mashed smooth

steps: Boil the potatoes whole in their skins on medium heat (3-4 whistles in a pressure cooker, or 20-25 minutes in a covered pot once the water returns to the boil) until a knife slides through easily. Peel them and let them cool completely.

While the potatoes cool, mix the atta with a little of the salt and add the water gradually, kneading into a soft, smooth dough that does not stick to your fingers. Cover and rest it for 20-30 minutes.

Grate or mash the potatoes until smooth with no lumps. Mix in the green chilli, ginger, coriander leaves, salt, red chilli powder, garam masala and amchur, plus the ajwain if using, and knead the filling briefly so it holds together. Taste for salt.
Divide the dough into balls and the filling into balls of about the same size (2 of each per serving).

Roll a dough ball into a 4-inch disc, keeping the edges thinner than the centre. Put a filling ball in the middle, gather the edges up over it, pinch to seal, pinch off any excess dough at the top and flatten gently with your palm.
Dust with atta and roll gently with light, even pressure into a 7-inch paratha. If the filling peeks through, patch it with a pinch of dry atta.
Heat a tawa on medium-high, then turn it to medium. Cook the paratha for 30-40 seconds until small bubbles appear and the underside has light spots, then flip.

Spread ghee over the top, flip again, spread ghee on the second side and press the edges with a spatula. Cook for about 1 minute per side until both sides have golden-brown spots and the paratha puffs.
Serve hot, topped with butter if using, alongside curd and pickle.
tips: Boil the potatoes whole in their skins so they stay dry; watery or lumpy filling is what tears the paratha while rolling.
Let the potatoes cool completely before mashing; warm filling makes the dough soft and sticky.
Roll from the centre outwards with very light pressure, turning the paratha a quarter turn now and then.

name: Aloo Shimla Mirch
steps: Rinse the potato cubes and drain well. Keep the capsicum pieces aside separately.
Heat the oil in a wide pan on medium heat. Add the cumin seeds and let them splutter for 20-30 seconds, then add the asafoetida and green chilli and stir for 10 seconds.

Add the potato, turmeric and salt and stir well. Cover and cook on low heat for 8-10 minutes, stirring every 2-3 minutes, until the potato is almost cooked (a knife meets only slight resistance at the centre) and the edges are turning golden.
Add the red chilli powder and coriander powder and stir for 30 seconds.
Add the capsicum, raise the heat to medium and stir-fry uncovered for 4-5 minutes, until the capsicum is just tender but still bright green with a slight crunch and the potato is fully cooked.
Sprinkle over the amchur and garam masala, toss for 30 seconds, check the salt and finish with the coriander leaves.
tips: Add the capsicum only after the potato is nearly done and never cover it: covered capsicum goes limp and turns dull olive.
Cut the potato small; that lets it cook through in the oil without any water.

name: Aloo Tikki
servesWith: green chutney and sweet tamarind chutney

ingredients.prep: boiled whole in the skin, peeled, cooled and mashed

steps: Pressure cook the whole, unpeeled potatoes with about a cup of water for 3 whistles on medium heat (or boil for 15-20 minutes) until a knife slides in easily. Drain and let the steam escape.
Peel the potatoes while warm, then let them cool completely - at least 30 minutes in the fridge. Cold, dry potatoes hold their shape; warm ones turn sticky.
Grate or mash the potatoes until smooth, with no lumps left.

Add the salt, green chilli, ginger, coriander leaves, red chilli powder, roasted cumin powder, garam masala, chaat masala, amchur and cornflour. Knead for a minute into a smooth dough that does not stick to your palm.
Grease your palms with a little oil, divide the dough into lemon-sized balls and flatten each into a patty about half an inch thick. Press any cracks at the edges smooth.
Heat a tawa or flat pan on medium heat and spread some of the oil. Place the tikkis and cook without moving them for 5-6 minutes, until the underside is deep golden and crisp.
Flip gently with a flat spatula, drizzle a little more oil around the edges and cook the other side for 4-5 minutes until equally crisp.
Serve hot with green chutney and sweet tamarind chutney.
tips: Waterlogged potatoes are why tikkis break: boil them in their skins, do not overcook, and let them cool fully before mashing.
Do not flip until a crust has formed - if the tikki sticks to the tawa, give it another minute.
If the mixture still feels soft, add cornflour a teaspoon at a time until it holds.

name: Aratikaya Vepudu

ingredients.prep: about 1 raw banana, peeled, cut into 1/2-inch cubes, kept in water
lightly crushed, added partway through frying

steps: Peel the raw bananas thinly with a knife, cut them into even 1/2-inch cubes and drop the cubes straight into a bowl of water so they do not blacken.

Bring a pot of water to the boil with the turmeric powder and a little of the salt. Drain the cubes, add them and cook for 3-4 minutes, only until a knife goes in with slight resistance. Drain and spread them on a plate to steam dry for 5 minutes.

Heat the oil in a wide pan on medium. Add the mustard seeds and, once they splutter, the cumin seeds, chana dal, urad dal and broken dry red chilli; fry until the dals turn golden, then add the curry leaves and let them crackle for a few seconds.

Add the banana cubes, spread them in a single layer and fry uncovered on medium for 10-12 minutes, turning every 2-3 minutes. After about 7 minutes add the crushed garlic, and keep frying until the cubes are golden and crisp on the outside and the garlic is golden.
Lower the heat, sprinkle over the red chilli powder, taste and add salt as needed, and toss for about 1 minute until every cube is evenly coated. Serve hot.
tips: Pull the cubes out of the boiling water while still firm; overcooked raw banana mashes in the pan and never crisps.
Rub a little oil on your hands and knife before peeling; the sap stains skin dark and is hard to wash off.
The cubes pick up only a little salt while boiling, so taste one and season the fry fully at the end.

name: Avial
aliases: kerala mixed vegetable coconut curd curry

ingredients.prep: peeled, cut into 2-inch batons, kept in water

steps: Cut all the vegetables into batons about 2 inches long and 1/2 inch thick, keeping them the same size; cut the drumstick, if using, into 2-inch pieces, splitting thick ones lengthwise. Drop the raw banana into water as you cut it so it does not blacken.
Grind the grated coconut, green chilli and cumin seeds to a coarse paste with 1-2 tablespoons of water - it should still look grainy, not smooth.
Whisk the sour curd until smooth with no lumps.
Put the drumstick, drained raw banana, carrot and beans in a wide pan with the turmeric powder, salt and a splash of water (about 1/4 cup for 2 servings). Cover and cook on medium for 6-7 minutes.
Add the pumpkin and cucumber, cover again and cook 4-5 minutes more, until all the vegetables are tender but still hold their shape and the water is mostly absorbed.
Add the coconut paste and fold it in gently. Cook uncovered on low for 2-3 minutes until the raw coconut smell goes.
Turn the heat to its lowest, add the whisked curd and fold it through gently for about a minute, just until heated - do not let it boil. Switch off.
Drizzle the coconut oil over the top, scatter the curry leaves (crushed lightly in your hand), cover and leave for 10 minutes, then mix gently and serve.
tips: Fold with a flat spatula or shake the pan instead of stirring - avial vegetables should stay as whole batons, not break into a mash.
Use sour, day-old curd and add it off the boil; boiling makes the curd split.
The raw coconut oil added at the end is the signature flavour - use coconut oil rather than any other oil.

name: Baingan Bharta

ingredients.prep: washed, dried and pricked a few times with a fork; roasted whole

steps: Rub the brinjal with a few drops of the oil. Roast it directly over a medium gas flame for 12-15 minutes, turning every 2-3 minutes with tongs, until the skin is charred and flaking all over and the brinjal has collapsed; a knife pushed into the thickest part near the stem should meet no resistance.

Put the roasted brinjal in a bowl, cover for 5 minutes, then peel off the charred skin with fingertips dipped in water and remove the stem. Mash the flesh with a fork; do not rinse it under the tap, as that washes away the smoky flavour.
Heat the rest of the oil in a kadai on medium heat. If using mustard oil, heat it until it just begins to smoke, then take it off the heat for a few seconds before continuing.
Add the cumin seeds and let them splutter for 20 seconds. Add the onion and saute for 4-5 minutes until translucent and just turning golden.
Add the ginger, garlic and green chilli and stir for 1 minute until the raw smell of garlic goes.

Turn the heat to low, add the turmeric, red chilli powder and coriander powder and stir for 15 seconds. Add the tomato and salt and cook for 5-6 minutes, mashing, until soft and the oil separates from the masala.
Add the mashed brinjal, mix well and cook on medium-low heat for 5-7 minutes, stirring often, until everything comes together and the excess moisture has dried off.
Stir in the garam masala if using, taste for salt, and finish with the coriander leaves.
tips: Pick a large, light, glossy brinjal with few seeds; heavy ones tend to be seedy and bitter.
Roast until it is completely soft right up to the stem; an under-roasted brinjal stays stringy and raw-tasting no matter how long you cook the masala.
No gas flame? Roast it in an oven at 220 C for 35-40 minutes, turning once. It cooks through, but you lose some of the smokiness.

name: Bangaladumpa Vepudu
servesWith: rice with pappu, sambar or rasam
steps: Peel the potatoes and cut them into even 1/2-inch cubes. Rinse twice in cold water to wash off the surface starch, drain and pat dry with a cloth.
Pound the garlic with the red chilli powder and a pinch of the salt into a coarse paste and keep it aside.
Heat the oil in a wide, heavy pan on medium. Add the mustard seeds and, once they splutter, the cumin seeds, chana dal and urad dal; fry until the dals turn golden, then add the curry leaves.

Add the potatoes, turmeric powder and the rest of the salt and toss to coat. Cover and cook on low for 10-12 minutes, stirring every 3 minutes, until a cube crushes easily when pressed with the spatula.
Uncover, raise the heat to medium and spread the potatoes in a single layer. Fry for 8-10 minutes, turning only every 2-3 minutes, until golden and crisp at the edges.
Lower the heat to low, add the garlic-chilli paste and toss for about 2 minutes, until the raw garlic smell is gone and every cube is coated. Serve hot.
tips: Rinse and dry the cubes well; surface starch and water make them stick and turn mushy instead of crisp.
Leave the potatoes alone between turns so a crust can form; constant stirring breaks them up.
Add the chilli-garlic paste only at the end; chilli powder burns within seconds in hot oil and turns bitter.

name: Beans Carrot Poriyal
aliases: beans carrot stir fry with coconut

ingredients.prep: topped and tailed, chopped into 1/4-inch pieces

steps: Chop the beans and carrot into the same small 1/4-inch pieces so they cook evenly.
Heat the oil in a kadai on medium. Add the mustard seeds; when they splutter, add the urad dal and fry about 30 seconds until light golden.
Add the dried red chilli (broken in two), curry leaves and asafoetida and stir for 10 seconds.

Add the beans, carrot and salt and toss well. Sprinkle 2-3 tablespoons of water for 2 servings (a little more for a bigger batch), cover and cook on low-medium for 8-10 minutes, stirring once or twice, until the beans are just tender with a slight bite and the carrot is cooked through.
Uncover and cook on medium for 1-2 minutes to dry off any water left in the pan.
Add the grated coconut, toss for 30 seconds and switch off.
tips: Keep the water to a sprinkle - poriyal is steamed in the pan, not boiled, and extra water makes it soggy and dull.
Add the coconut only at the end; cooking it longer dries it out and it loses its sweetness.

name: Beerakaya Pappu
servesWith: hot rice, with a vegetable fry on the side

ingredients.prep: hard ridges scraped off, cut into 1-inch pieces

steps: Rinse the toor dal 2-3 times until the water runs nearly clear. Soak the tamarind in just enough warm water to cover it.
Scrape only the hard ridges off the ridge gourd, leaving the soft green skin, and taste a tiny raw piece; if it is bitter, discard that gourd. Cut the rest into 1-inch pieces.

Put the dal, water, ridge gourd, onion, green chillies, turmeric powder and a few drops of the oil into a pressure cooker. Cook on medium heat for 4 whistles, then let the pressure drop on its own, about 10 minutes.

Open the cooker and mash the dal with a ladle or pappu gutti until creamy; the gourd will partly break down, which is right. Squeeze the tamarind, add its pulp and the salt, and simmer on low for 3-4 minutes, stirring, adding hot water if needed until the dal is thick but pourable.

For the tempering, heat the remaining oil in a small pan on medium. Add the mustard seeds and, once they splutter, the cumin seeds, dry red chilli and garlic; fry until the garlic is golden, about 30 seconds. Turn off the heat and stir in the curry leaves and asafoetida.
Pour the tempering over the dal, add the coriander leaves, cover for 2 minutes and stir before serving.
tips: Always taste a raw sliver of the ridge gourd; a bitter one can make you ill and ruins the whole pot, so throw it away rather than cook it.
Add the tamarind only after the dal is cooked and mashed; acid in the cooker slows the dal's softening and can leave it grainy.
If the dal is still grainy after cooking, close the cooker and give it one more whistle before mashing.

name: Beetroot Poriyal
steps: Peel the beetroot and chop it into small 1/4-inch cubes, or grate it for a quicker version.
Heat the oil in a kadai on medium. Add the mustard seeds; when they splutter, add the urad dal and fry about 30 seconds until light golden.
Add the green chilli, curry leaves and asafoetida and stir for 10 seconds.

Add the beetroot and salt and toss. Sprinkle about 1/4 cup of water for 2 servings (more for a bigger batch, about half that if grated), cover and cook on low for 10-12 minutes (5-6 minutes if grated), stirring every few minutes and adding a splash more water if the pan runs dry, until a piece yields easily when pressed with a spoon.
Uncover and cook on medium for 1-2 minutes until any water has dried off.
Add the grated coconut, toss for 30 seconds and switch off.
tips: Chop the beetroot small and even - large pieces stay hard long after the rest is done.
Leave out turmeric; it dulls the beetroot's colour.
Rub a few drops of oil on your hands and board before chopping to keep the stains off.

name: Bendakaya Fry
servesWith: hot rice with pappu or rasam

ingredients.prep: washed, dried completely, cut into 1 cm rounds

steps: Wash the okra and dry every piece completely with a cloth, then trim the tops and tails and cut into 1 cm rounds.

Heat the oil in a wide pan or kadai on medium. Add the mustard seeds and, once they splutter, the cumin seeds, chana dal, urad dal and broken dry red chilli; fry for 30-40 seconds until the dals turn golden. Add the curry leaves and let them crackle for a few seconds.
Add the okra and turmeric powder, toss to coat everything in the oil and spread it out in an even layer.

Cook uncovered on medium for 15-18 minutes, stirring gently every 2-3 minutes. When the okra has lost its stickiness (about 12 minutes in), add the crushed garlic and keep frying until the rounds have shrunk, the edges are browned and crisp and the garlic is golden. Do not cover the pan at any point.
Lower the heat, add the salt, red chilli powder and peanut powder if using, and toss for about 1 minute until evenly coated. Serve hot.
tips: Dry the okra fully before cutting; any water on it turns the fry slimy.
Add salt only at the end; salted early, okra lets out moisture and steams soft instead of crisping.
Use a wide pan so the okra sits in a thin layer; crowded, it stews. For larger amounts fry in two batches.

name: Bhindi Fry

ingredients.prep: washed, dried completely, ends trimmed, cut into 1/2-inch rounds

steps: Wash the okra, then dry each pod completely with a cloth (or leave it spread out to air-dry). Trim the top and tail and cut into rounds.
Heat the oil in a wide heavy pan or cast-iron kadai on medium-high heat. Add the cumin seeds and let them splutter for 20 seconds.

Add the okra and spread it out in a single layer. Cook uncovered on medium heat for 12-15 minutes, turning gently every 2 minutes, until the stickiness is gone, the pieces have shrunk and the edges are golden brown and crisp.
Turn the heat to low, sprinkle over the turmeric, red chilli powder, coriander powder and salt, and toss for 1-2 minutes so the spices cook without burning.
Sprinkle over the amchur, toss for 30 seconds and turn off the heat. Serve straight away, as it softens as it sits.
tips: Add the salt only at the end; salted early, okra releases moisture and turns slimy instead of crisp.
Use your widest pan and do not crowd it or cover it; if the okra is piled up it steams rather than fries. For more than 2 servings, fry it in two batches and combine before adding the spices.
Stir only every couple of minutes; constant stirring breaks the rounds and keeps them from browning.

name: Bhindi Masala

ingredients.prep: washed, dried completely, ends trimmed, cut into 1-inch pieces

steps: Wash the okra and dry every pod completely with a cloth before cutting; any water left on it makes the dish slimy. Trim the ends and cut into pieces.

Heat two-thirds of the oil in a wide pan on medium-high heat. Add the okra in a single layer and fry uncovered for 8-10 minutes, stirring every couple of minutes, until it is no longer sticky, the edges are browned and it is tender. Do not salt it yet. Remove to a plate.
In the same pan, heat the remaining oil on medium heat. Add the cumin seeds and let them splutter for 20 seconds.
Add the onion and saute for 4-5 minutes until light golden. Add the ginger, garlic and green chilli and stir for 1 minute until the raw smell goes.

Turn the heat to low, add the turmeric, red chilli powder and coriander powder and stir for 20 seconds. Add the tomato and salt and cook for 4-5 minutes until the tomato breaks down and the oil separates from the masala.
Return the fried okra to the pan, add the amchur and garam masala and toss gently on medium heat for 2-3 minutes until every piece is coated. Do not cover.
Taste for salt, turn off the heat and finish with the coriander leaves.
tips: Dry the okra fully before cutting and never cover the pan; trapped steam is what makes bhindi slimy.
Salt goes into the masala, not onto the frying okra: salt pulls out moisture and brings the slime back.
Fry the okra in batches if your pan is small; piled up, it steams instead of frying.

name: Garlic Broccoli Stir-fry
servesWith: Veg Fried Rice or Hakka Noodles, or as a side

ingredients.prep: cut into bite-size florets; thick stem peeled and thinly sliced

steps: Cut the broccoli into bite-size florets, keeping a little stem on each. Peel the thick main stem and slice it thin; it cooks the same as the florets. Finely chop the garlic and slice the spring onion greens.
Soak the florets in warm salted water for 10 minutes to draw out any hidden insects, then rinse and drain.

Bring a pot of salted water to a boil, add the broccoli and boil for about 2 minutes, just until it turns bright green. Drain, rinse under cold water to stop the cooking, and shake the colander until no water clings to the florets.
Heat the oil in a wok or wide pan on high heat until it shimmers. Add the well-drained broccoli and toss for about 2 minutes, until it is hot through and lightly charred at the edges.

Lower the heat to medium, push the broccoli to the sides, add the garlic and the chilli flakes if using to the cleared centre and stir for 30-45 seconds, until the garlic is pale golden and fragrant, then toss everything together.
Add the soy sauce, pepper, sugar if using and a little salt, and toss. If using cornflour, stir it into 2 tablespoons of water, pour it in and toss for 30 seconds until it forms a light glossy coat.
Turn off the heat, scatter the spring onion greens and serve immediately.
tips: Stop cooking while the broccoli is still bright green with a bite; dull olive-green means it is overdone.
Drain the blanched broccoli well so it sears in the wok instead of steaming.
Take the garlic only to pale golden; dark brown garlic turns the whole dish bitter.

name: Cabbage Fry
servesWith: rice with pappu or rasam, or chapati
steps: Shred the cabbage finely and evenly, rinse it in a colander and let it drain well.

Heat the oil in a kadai on medium. Add the mustard seeds and, once they splutter, the cumin seeds, chana dal, urad dal and broken dry red chilli; fry until the dals turn golden, then add the curry leaves and asafoetida.
Add the onion and green chillies and saute for 2-3 minutes until the onion is soft and translucent.

Add the cabbage, turmeric powder and salt and toss well. Cover and cook on low for 5-6 minutes, stirring once or twice, until the cabbage wilts and turns just tender; do not add water, it steams in its own moisture.
Uncover, raise the heat to medium and stir-fry for 2-3 minutes to drive off the remaining moisture. The cabbage should be tender with a slight bite, not mushy.
Scatter the coriander leaves over and serve hot.
tips: Shred the cabbage fine and even so it cooks in minutes; thick pieces need water and go soggy.
Stop cooking while it still has a slight bite; overcooked cabbage turns limp and smells sulphurous.

name: Patta Gobi Matar

ingredients.prep: outer leaves and core removed, finely shredded

steps: Shred the cabbage finely into thin strips, rinse and drain it well in a colander. Shell the peas if using fresh.
Heat the oil in a kadai on medium heat. Add the cumin seeds and let them splutter for 20 seconds, then add the asafoetida, ginger and green chilli and stir for 30 seconds.
If using fresh peas, add them with a tablespoon of water, cover and cook for 3-4 minutes until they start to soften, since they take longer than the cabbage.
Turn the heat to low, add the turmeric, red chilli powder and coriander powder and stir for 10 seconds. Add the tomato and cook for 2-3 minutes until soft.

Add the cabbage and salt and toss well. Cover and cook on low-medium heat for 6-8 minutes, stirring twice, without adding water; the cabbage releases its own. If using frozen peas, add them now with the cabbage.
Uncover, raise the heat to medium-high and stir for 2-3 minutes until the moisture has dried off and the cabbage is tender with a slight bite.
Sprinkle the garam masala if using, toss, and finish with the coriander leaves.
tips: Do not overcook: cabbage that is cooked to softness goes watery and smells sulphurous. Stop while it still has a little bite.
Do not add water to the cabbage; drain it well after washing and finish uncovered so the sabzi ends dry.

name: Cabbage Poriyal
steps: Shred the cabbage finely into thin strips about 1 inch long, rinse and drain well.
Heat the oil in a kadai on medium. Add the mustard seeds; when they splutter, add the chana dal and fry for 20 seconds, then add the urad dal and fry another 30 seconds until both are golden.
Add the green chilli, curry leaves and asafoetida and stir for 10 seconds.
Add the cabbage, turmeric powder and salt and toss on medium-high for 2 minutes.
Cover and cook on low for 5-7 minutes, stirring once or twice, until the cabbage is tender with a slight bite - no water is needed, it steams in its own moisture.
Uncover and cook 1 minute to dry off any liquid, then add the grated coconut, mix well and switch off.
tips: Don't add water or overcook - stewed cabbage turns watery and develops a strong sulphur smell.
Shred it evenly thin so all of it is done at the same moment.

name: Capsicum Senagapindi Kura
steps: In a dry pan on low heat, roast the besan for 3-4 minutes, stirring constantly, until it smells nutty and turns a shade darker. Tip it onto a plate.
Heat the oil in the same pan on medium. Add the mustard seeds and, once they splutter, the cumin seeds, chana dal and urad dal; fry until the dals turn golden, then add the curry leaves.
Add the onion and green chillies and saute for 2-3 minutes until the onion softens.
Add the capsicum, turmeric powder and salt and stir-fry uncovered on medium for 4-5 minutes, until the capsicum is just tender but still bright green with a slight crunch.
Stir in the red chilli powder and coriander powder, then sprinkle the roasted besan over in 2-3 additions, tossing after each so it coats the pieces instead of clumping.

Sprinkle the water over, lower the heat and cook for 3-4 minutes, stirring often, until the besan is crumbly, clings to the capsicum and no longer smells raw. Scatter the coriander leaves over and serve.
tips: Roast the besan first; under-cooked besan tastes raw and slightly bitter and sits in pasty lumps.
Sprinkle the besan a little at a time over the capsicum rather than dumping it in one heap, which forms lumps.
Do not cook the capsicum soft before the besan goes in; it keeps cooking in the last few minutes.

name: Chilli Mushroom
servesWith: Veg Fried Rice or Hakka Noodles, or on its own as a starter

ingredients.prep: wiped clean; halve small ones, quarter large ones
cut into 1-inch squares, layers separated into petals
chopped, whites and greens kept separate

steps: Wipe the mushrooms with a damp cloth, or rinse them quickly and pat them completely dry; never soak them. Trim the stem ends, halve small mushrooms and quarter large ones.

Cut the onion and capsicum into 1-inch squares and separate the onion layers into petals. Finely chop the garlic and ginger, slit the green chillies, and keep the spring onion whites and greens separate.

Heat the oil for deep frying in a kadai on medium-high heat. While it heats, mix the cornflour for the batter, maida, a pinch of the pepper and a little salt with just enough water to make a thick batter, then add the mushrooms and coat them evenly.
When a drop of batter rises at once with steady bubbles, fry the mushrooms in batches for 3-4 minutes, turning them, until golden and crisp. Drain on paper.

In a wok, heat the oil for the sauce on high heat. Add the garlic, ginger and green chillies and stir for 30 seconds. Add the onion petals and spring onion whites and toss for 1 minute, then add the capsicum and toss for 1 minute more; the onion and capsicum should stay crunchy.

Add the soy sauce, red chilli sauce, vinegar, the ketchup if using and the rest of the pepper, and stir for 30 seconds. Stir the cornflour for the sauce into 2-3 tablespoons of water, pour it in and stir until thick and glossy, about 30 seconds.
Add the fried mushrooms and toss on high heat for about 1 minute until coated. Turn off the heat, add the spring onion greens and serve at once.
tips: Do not soak mushrooms in water; they absorb it and the coating will not crisp.
Coat the mushrooms only just before frying, because salted mushrooms start releasing water within minutes.
Keep the onion and capsicum on high heat for no more than 2 minutes so they stay crunchy.

name: Green Coriander Chutney

ingredients.prep: leaves and tender stems, washed well

ingredients.item: roasted chana dal (bhuna chana dal / pottukadalai / putnalu)

steps: Pick the coriander: keep the leaves and tender upper stems, and discard the thick lower stems and roots.
Wash the coriander and mint leaves in a large bowl of water 2-3 times, lifting them out each time so the grit stays behind. Drain well.
Put the coriander, mint leaves, green chilli, ginger, cumin seeds, roasted chana dal, salt, sugar, lemon juice and ice-cold water into a small grinder jar.
Grind in short pulses, scraping down the sides in between, to a smooth, thick paste. Add more cold water a teaspoon at a time only if the blades do not catch.
Taste and adjust salt and lemon juice. Transfer to a clean container and refrigerate; it keeps for 2-3 days.
tips: Ice-cold water and lemon juice keep the chutney bright green; grinding for long stretches heats it and turns it dark.
Keep it thick for sandwiches, and thin it with a little water for chaat.
Roasted chana dal gives body and stops the chutney from separating into water and paste.

name: Cucumber Kosambari
servesWith: a South Indian rice meal, or on its own as a light snack

ingredients.prep: finely diced; peeled and deseeded if the skin is thick or it is very watery

steps: Rinse the moong dal and soak it in water for 45-60 minutes (or 20-30 minutes in hot water), until the grains bite through easily but still hold their shape. Drain completely.
Dice the cucumber small; if it is very watery, scoop out the seeds first.
Heat the oil in a small pan on medium, add the mustard seeds and let them splutter, then add the curry leaves and asafoetida. Switch off and let it cool.
Just before serving, combine the drained moong dal, cucumber, green chilli, grated coconut and coriander leaves in a bowl.
Pour the tempering over, add the salt and lemon juice, toss and serve immediately.
tips: Add salt and lemon only at the last minute - salt pulls water out of the cucumber and leaves the salad sitting in a puddle.
Don't cook the moong dal; soak it just until tender to the bite - over-soaked dal goes mushy.

name: Cucumber Raita
steps: Wash the cucumber and taste the stem end; peel it if it is bitter or the skin is thick. Grate it on the large holes of a grater.
Gently squeeze the grated cucumber in your palm to remove the excess water, keeping the juice aside.
Whisk the curd in a bowl until completely smooth. If it is very thick, loosen it with a little of the cucumber juice or cold water.
Add the grated cucumber, roasted cumin powder, red chilli powder, sugar, finely chopped mint leaves and most of the coriander leaves. Mix gently.
If time allows, chill for 15 minutes. Stir in the salt just before serving and top with the remaining coriander leaves and a pinch more roasted cumin powder.
tips: Use fresh, chilled curd - sour curd makes the raita sharp.
Add salt only when serving; salted cucumber keeps releasing water and thins the raita.
For the best roasted cumin powder, dry-roast cumin seeds on low heat for 1-2 minutes until a shade darker, then crush them.

name: Dal Palak

ingredients.prep: thick stems removed, washed well, finely chopped

steps: Rinse the toor dal in 2-3 changes of water. Pressure-cook it with the water and turmeric powder on medium heat for 4 whistles until completely soft. Let the pressure release on its own and mash the dal.
While the dal cooks, wash the spinach in a large bowl of water, lifting the leaves out so the grit stays at the bottom; repeat 2-3 times, then chop finely.

Heat the ghee in a kadai on medium heat. Add the cumin seeds and asafoetida; when the cumin crackles, add the garlic and dried red chilli and fry for 20-30 seconds until the garlic smells fragrant but has not yet coloured.
Add the onion and fry for 4-5 minutes until light golden. Add the ginger and green chilli, then the tomato and kashmiri red chilli powder, and cook for 4-5 minutes until the tomato is soft.
Add the spinach and stir for 2-3 minutes until it wilts completely.
Pour in the mashed dal, add salt and enough hot water for a medium-thick consistency. Simmer on low heat for 5-6 minutes, stirring now and then.
Switch off the heat, stir in the lemon juice if using, and serve hot.
tips: Add the spinach after the masala rather than pressure-cooking it with the dal; that keeps it green and fresh-tasting.
Spinach hides grit; lift it out of the washing water rather than pouring the water off, or the sand goes back on the leaves.

name: Dal Tadka
servesWith: steamed rice or jeera rice, or roti
steps: Rinse the toor dal in 2-3 changes of water until the water runs mostly clear. Soak it for 20-30 minutes if you have time.
Pressure-cook the dal with the water and turmeric powder on medium heat for 4-5 whistles (3 if soaked), until completely soft. Let the pressure release on its own, then whisk the dal smooth.
Heat half the ghee in a pan on medium heat. Add half the cumin seeds; when they crackle, add the onion and fry for 4-5 minutes until light golden.
Add the ginger and green chilli and saute for 30 seconds, then add the tomato and cook for 4-5 minutes until soft and mushy.
Pour in the cooked dal, add salt and stir. Simmer on low heat for 5 minutes, adding hot water as needed; it should be pourable, not pasty.

For the tadka, heat the remaining ghee in a small pan on medium heat. Add the remaining cumin seeds; when they crackle, add the garlic and fry for about 1 minute until it turns golden. Add the dried red chilli and asafoetida, switch off the heat and stir in the kashmiri red chilli powder.
Pour the sizzling tadka over the dal straight away, cover for a minute to trap the aroma, then garnish with coriander leaves and serve hot.
tips: Cook the dal until it is completely soft; undercooked toor dal never whisks smooth.
Switch off the heat before adding the chilli powder to the tadka; it burns in seconds and turns the dal bitter.
Dal thickens as it stands, so loosen it with hot water before serving.

name: Dum Aloo

ingredients.prep: small baby potatoes, scrubbed (or medium potatoes, quartered)

steps: Boil the baby potatoes in salted water for 10-12 minutes (or pressure-cook for 1 whistle on high and release the pressure straight away) until a knife goes in with slight resistance. Drain, cool, peel and prick each one all over with a fork.
Heat the oil in a kadai on medium heat and fry the potatoes for 6-8 minutes, turning, until golden and lightly crisp. Lift them out and keep the oil in the pan.
Grind the onion to a smooth paste. Separately grind the tomato, ginger, garlic, green chilli and cashews to a smooth puree.
In the same oil, add the bay leaf and cumin seeds; when they sizzle, add the onion paste and fry on medium heat for 8-10 minutes, stirring, until golden brown and the raw smell is gone.
Add the turmeric powder, kashmiri red chilli powder and coriander powder and stir for 20 seconds. Add the tomato-cashew puree and salt and cook for 6-8 minutes until thick and oil separates.
Turn the heat to the lowest. Whisk the curd smooth and add it a spoonful at a time, stirring continuously, then cook for 2-3 minutes.
Add the water and garam masala, bring to a gentle simmer and add the fried potatoes. Cover tightly and cook on the lowest heat (dum) for 10-12 minutes so the potatoes soak up the gravy.
Stir in the kasuri methi crushed between your palms, garnish with coriander leaves and serve hot.
tips: Prick the boiled potatoes all over before frying; the holes are what let the gravy seep in during the dum.
Always drop the heat to the lowest and add the curd whisked and a little at a time, or it splits into grainy bits.
Do not overboil the potatoes; soft ones break apart when you fry them.

name: Garden Lettuce Salad

ingredients.prep: leaves washed, dried and torn into bite-size pieces
peeled and grated or shaved into ribbons

steps: Separate the lettuce leaves and wash them in a bowl of cold water, lifting them out so the grit stays behind. If the leaves are limp, soak them in ice-cold water for 10 minutes to crisp them.
Dry the leaves thoroughly in a salad spinner or by patting them between clean kitchen towels, then tear them by hand into bite-size pieces. Keep them in the fridge until serving.
Slice the cucumber into thin rounds, cut the tomato into wedges, grate the carrot or shave it into ribbons with a peeler, and slice the onion into thin rings.
Make the dressing: whisk the olive oil, lemon juice, the mustard sauce and sugar if using, salt and pepper in a small bowl, or shake them in a closed jar, until slightly thickened and well combined.
Just before serving, put the lettuce and vegetables in a large bowl, pour over the dressing and toss gently with your hands or two spoons until the leaves are lightly coated. Serve at once.
tips: Dry the lettuce completely; dressing slides off wet leaves and the salad turns watery.
Dress the salad only at the table, because the salt wilts lettuce within minutes.
Taste the dressing on a lettuce leaf rather than from the spoon before you adjust it.

name: Gobi Manchurian
servesWith: Veg Fried Rice or Hakka Noodles, or on its own as a starter

ingredients.prep: cut into bite-size florets about 1.5 inches across
chopped, whites and greens kept separate

steps: Bring a pot of salted water to a boil, add the cauliflower florets and boil for 2 minutes, just until they lose their raw crunch. Drain, spread on a clean cloth and let them dry completely, about 10 minutes.
Meanwhile finely chop the ginger, garlic and green chilli, cut the capsicum into small squares, and keep the spring onion whites and greens separate.

In a bowl mix the maida, cornflour for the batter, Kashmiri chilli powder, pepper, salt and about a third of the chopped ginger and garlic. Add water a little at a time and whisk to a thick, smooth batter that coats a spoon and drips off slowly. Add the dry florets and toss until each one is coated.

Heat the oil for deep frying in a kadai on medium-high heat until a drop of batter rises to the top at once with steady bubbles. Fry the florets in batches, without crowding, for 4-5 minutes, turning them, until golden and crisp. Drain on paper.

In a wok, heat the oil for the sauce on high heat. Add the remaining ginger and garlic, the green chilli and the spring onion whites and stir for 30 seconds until fragrant. Add the capsicum and toss for 1 minute.

Add the soy sauce, red chilli sauce, tomato ketchup and vinegar with a small pinch of salt and stir for 30 seconds. Stir the cornflour for the sauce into 2-3 tablespoons of water, pour it in and stir until the sauce turns thick and glossy, about 30 seconds.

Add the fried gobi and toss on high heat for about 1 minute, until every piece is coated and no liquid is left at the bottom of the wok. Turn off the heat, scatter the spring onion greens and serve immediately.
tips: Dry the blanched florets completely; wet florets make the batter slide off and the oil spit.
Toss the fried gobi into the sauce only just before serving, because it loses its crispness within minutes.
Keep the cornflour slurry small for the dry version; more slurry and water turns it into gravy Manchurian.

name: Gobi Matar
steps: Soak the cauliflower florets in warm salted water for 10 minutes to clean them, then drain and pat dry. Shell the peas if using fresh.
Heat the oil in a kadai on medium heat. Add the cumin seeds and let them splutter for 20-30 seconds, then add the asafoetida, ginger and green chilli and stir for 30 seconds.
Turn the heat to low, add the turmeric, red chilli powder and coriander powder and stir for 15 seconds. Add the tomato and cook for 3-4 minutes until soft and pulpy.
Add the cauliflower, fresh peas and salt and toss on medium heat for 2 minutes until the florets are coated in the masala.

Cover and cook on low heat for 10-12 minutes without adding water, turning gently every 3-4 minutes, until a knife slides easily into the stem of a floret but the florets still hold their shape. If using frozen peas, stir them in for the last 4 minutes.
Uncover and cook on medium heat for 2-3 minutes to dry off any moisture and lightly brown the edges.
Sprinkle over the garam masala, toss, and finish with the coriander leaves.
tips: Stop cooking as soon as the florets are tender; overcooked cauliflower goes mushy and smells strongly of sulphur.
Keep the florets small and even so they cook in their own steam without any water.
Toss by folding from the bottom rather than stirring, so the florets do not break.

name: Gobi Paratha

ingredients.prep: florets washed, patted dry and finely grated

steps: Mix the atta with a little of the salt and add the water gradually, kneading into a soft, smooth dough. Cover and rest it for 20-30 minutes.
Wash the cauliflower florets, pat them completely dry with a cloth, and grate them finely (or pulse in a chopper) into rice-sized bits, leaving out the thick stem.
Mix the grated cauliflower with the green chilli, ginger, coriander leaves, red chilli powder, garam masala, amchur and ajwain. Do not add salt yet.
Divide the dough into balls (2 per serving). Just before you start stuffing, mix salt into the filling; if it releases water, squeeze the filling firmly in your fist and discard the liquid.
Roll a dough ball into a 4-inch disc with thinner edges. Pile a portion of filling in the centre, gather the edges over it, pinch to seal, remove the excess dough on top and flatten gently.
Dust with atta and roll gently into a 7-inch paratha, patching any tear with a pinch of dry atta.
Heat a tawa on medium-high, then turn it to medium. Cook the paratha for 30-40 seconds until bubbles appear, then flip.
Spread ghee on both sides one at a time, pressing the edges with a spatula, and cook for about 1 minute per side until golden-brown spots appear all over and the filling is cooked through. Serve hot.
tips: Salt makes grated cauliflower weep, so add it only just before stuffing and squeeze out any water; wet filling bursts through the dough.
Grate the cauliflower fine; coarse pieces poke holes in the paratha while rolling.
Dry the florets thoroughly after washing; leftover water has the same effect as salt.

name: Guacamole

ingredients.prep: halved, seeded and flesh scooped out
seeds and watery pulp removed, finely chopped

steps: Finely chop the onion. If it is very sharp, rinse it in cold water and drain it well.
Halve the tomato, scoop out the seeds and watery pulp, and chop the flesh finely. Finely chop the green chilli, removing the seeds for less heat, and the coriander.
Check the avocado is ripe: it should yield to gentle pressure. Cut it lengthwise around the seed, twist the halves apart, remove the seed and scoop the flesh into a bowl.
Add the lemon juice and salt and mash with a fork to a chunky texture, leaving some small pieces.
Fold in the onion, tomato, green chilli and coriander. Taste and adjust the salt and lemon juice.
Serve straight away. To hold it for up to 2 hours, press cling film directly onto the surface and refrigerate.
tips: Use properly ripe avocados; hard ones will not mash and taste grassy. Ripen them at room temperature in a paper bag for 1-3 days.
Mix in the lemon juice as soon as the flesh is in the bowl and keep the surface covered, or it turns brown.
Deseed the tomato so the guacamole does not turn watery.

name: Gutti Vankaya Kura

ingredients.prep: 3-4 small ones, stems on, slit into four from the base

steps: Rinse the brinjals and keep the stems on. Slit each one into four from the base up, stopping about 1 cm short of the stem so the quarters stay joined, and drop them into a bowl of salted water so they do not darken.
Soak the tamarind in just enough hot water to cover it for 10 minutes, then squeeze it and keep the pulp and liquid; discard the fibre and seeds.

In a dry pan on medium-low, roast the peanuts for 4-5 minutes, stirring, until they crackle and the skins blister; tip them out. Roast the coriander seeds for about 1 minute, add the cumin seeds for 30 seconds, then the sesame seeds for about 1 minute, stirring, until they start to pop, and add the dry coconut, if using, for the last 30 seconds. Tip everything onto a plate at once so it stops browning, and let it cool.

Grind the roasted mix to a coarse powder. Add the onion, garlic, tamarind pulp, jaggery, turmeric powder, red chilli powder and salt, and grind to a thick, coarse paste, adding water only a teaspoon at a time if the blender will not turn.
Drain the brinjals, pat them dry and press the paste deep into each slit, closing the quarters back up. Keep whatever paste is left over.
Heat the oil in a wide, heavy pan on medium. Add the mustard seeds and, once they splutter, the curry leaves. Lay the stuffed brinjals in the pan in a single layer.
Cover and cook on low for 15-18 minutes, turning each brinjal gently every 4-5 minutes, until a knife slides easily through the thickest part near the stem.

Loosen the leftover paste with the water, pour it around the brinjals, cover and simmer on low for 8-10 minutes, stirring the gravy (not the brinjals) once or twice, until the raw onion smell is gone, the gravy is thick and oil shines at the edges. Taste for salt, scatter the coriander leaves and rest it covered for 5 minutes before serving.
tips: Choose small, glossy brinjals with fresh green stems; large or seedy ones stay tough in the middle and can taste bitter.
Keep the stuffing thick and coarse; a wet, smooth paste slides out of the slits into the pan and scorches.
Cook low and covered, and turn the brinjals rather than stirring, so the peanut masala does not catch and the brinjals stay whole.

name: Hare Pyaz ki Sabzi

ingredients.prep: roots trimmed, white bulbs and green leaves finely chopped and kept separate

steps: Wash the spring onions well, paying attention to the root end where grit collects. Trim the roots, then finely chop the white bulbs and the green leaves, keeping them in separate piles.
Heat the oil in a kadhai on medium. Add the cumin seeds and hing and let them crackle.
Add the chopped whites and green chilli and saute 2-3 minutes until soft and translucent.

Add the turmeric, red chilli powder and coriander powder and stir for 15 seconds. Add the chopped greens and salt and cook uncovered 2-3 minutes, stirring, until they have just wilted but are still moist; the besan needs that moisture to cook in.
Turn the heat to low. Sprinkle the besan evenly over the onions while stirring continuously, so it coats them without forming lumps.

Keep cooking on low for 6-8 minutes, stirring constantly, until the besan turns a shade darker, smells nutty with no raw smell, and the sabzi looks crumbly. If it looks dry and powdery, sprinkle a splash of water and stir for another 1-2 minutes.
Stir in the amchur if using and serve hot.
tips: Keep the heat low once the besan goes in and never stop stirring; it scorches within seconds and turns bitter.
Taste a pinch before serving: if the besan still tastes raw or sticks to the palate, cook it a few minutes longer.
Salt sparingly, as a big pile of spring onion greens cooks down to a small amount.

name: Jeera Aloo
servesWith: puri or roti, or as a side with dal-rice

ingredients.prep: boiled until just tender, cooled, peeled and cut into 1-inch cubes

steps: Boil the potato whole in its skin: pressure cook for 2 whistles on medium heat, or simmer in a covered pot for 15-20 minutes, until a knife goes in with slight resistance at the centre. Do not overcook.
Let the potato cool completely (30 minutes, or 15 minutes in the fridge), then peel and cut into cubes.
Heat the oil in a kadai or wide pan on medium heat. Add the cumin seeds and let them sizzle for 30-40 seconds until they turn a shade darker and smell toasty, without letting them blacken.
Add the green chilli and ginger and stir for 20-30 seconds.
Turn the heat to low and add the turmeric, red chilli powder and coriander powder; stir for 10 seconds so they do not burn.
Add the potato cubes and salt and toss gently to coat. Raise the heat to medium-high and cook for 5-7 minutes, tossing every minute, until the edges turn golden and slightly crisp.
Sprinkle over the amchur and toss once more. Turn off the heat, add the coriander leaves, and squeeze over the lemon juice if using.
tips: Use fully cooled boiled potatoes; warm ones crumble into mash when tossed. Potatoes boiled a few hours ahead, or the night before, and kept in the fridge are ideal.
Be generous with the cumin and let it sizzle properly, but pull it the moment it darkens: burnt cumin makes the whole dish bitter.
Toss by shaking the pan or folding gently rather than stirring hard, so the cubes keep their edges.

name: Kachumber Salad

ingredients.prep: deseeded and cut into small 1/4-inch dice

steps: Wash the cucumber and taste a slice from the stem end; peel it if the skin is bitter or waxy. If the seeds are very watery, scoop them out, then cut into small quarter-inch dice.
Halve the tomato, scoop out the seeds and pulp, and dice the flesh to the same size as the cucumber.
Finely chop the onion. If it is very sharp, soak it in cold water for 5 minutes and drain it well.
Finely chop the green chilli and coriander leaves.
Just before serving, put everything in a bowl, add the salt, roasted cumin powder, chaat masala, black pepper powder and lemon juice, and toss well.
Taste, adjust the salt and lemon juice, and serve immediately.
tips: Add the salt only at the last minute - salt draws water out of the vegetables and turns the salad soggy within 15 minutes.
Deseeding the tomato (and a watery cucumber) keeps the salad crunchy instead of sitting in juice.

name: Khatta Meetha Kaddu ki Sabzi

ingredients.prep: seeds and stringy pulp removed, cut into 1-inch cubes; peel only if the skin is hard

steps: Scoop out the seeds and stringy pulp from the pumpkin and cut it into 1-inch cubes. Peel it only if the skin is hard; on a young pumpkin the skin can stay on and helps the pieces hold together.

Heat the oil in a kadhai on medium (if using mustard oil, heat it until it just smokes, then let it cool for 30 seconds). Add the fenugreek seeds, cumin seeds, fennel seeds, kalonji (if using), dried red chilli (if using) and hing and fry for 15-20 seconds, only until the fenugreek turns reddish-brown.
Add the ginger and green chilli and saute for 30 seconds.
Add the pumpkin, turmeric, red chilli powder, coriander powder and salt, and toss on medium heat for 2 minutes so the spices coat every piece.
Add a splash of water, cover and cook on low for 12-15 minutes, stirring every 4-5 minutes, until the pumpkin is soft enough to crush with the spoon.
Mash the pumpkin roughly with the back of the ladle, leaving some chunks. Stir in the jaggery and amchur and cook uncovered 3-4 minutes until the jaggery melts and the sabzi turns thick and glossy.
Taste and balance with a little more amchur or jaggery; it should be clearly both sweet and tangy. Stir in the garam masala, scatter the coriander leaves and serve.
tips: Watch the fenugreek seeds: once they go black they turn the whole dish bitter, so have the ginger ready and move on as soon as they redden.
Pumpkin carries its own water; add only a splash to start, or it becomes a runny mash.
This is the puri-and-kaddu of weddings and temple bhandaras; it tastes even better an hour after cooking, once the sweet and sour settle.

name: Kakarakaya Fry
servesWith: hot rice with pappu or rasam

ingredients.prep: cut into thin 3-4 mm rounds, hard seeds removed

steps: Wash the bitter gourds, trim the ends and cut into thin rounds of even thickness, 3-4 mm. Pick out any hard, reddish seeds; soft white ones can stay.

Toss the rounds with the turmeric powder and about 1/2 teaspoon of the salt for every 250 g of bitter gourd, and leave for 20 minutes. Squeeze them firmly by the handful and throw away the bitter juice.
Pound or pulse the roasted peanuts, garlic, cumin seeds, red chilli powder and jaggery into a coarse powder, not a paste.
Heat the oil in a wide pan on medium. Add the mustard seeds and, once they splutter, the curry leaves, then spread the squeezed bitter gourd in the pan.
Fry uncovered on medium for 15-18 minutes, stirring every 2-3 minutes, until the rounds are deep golden, shrunk and crisp at the edges; they crisp further as they cool.
Lower the heat, sprinkle over the peanut-garlic powder, taste before adding any more salt, and toss for 1-2 minutes until fragrant. Serve hot.
tips: Squeeze hard after salting; that juice carries much of the bitterness, and drier slices crisp instead of steaming.
The slices are already salted, so taste before adding more at the end.
Keep every round the same thickness so they all crisp together without some burning.

name: Karela Fry

ingredients.prep: ridges lightly scraped, cut into thin 1/4-inch rounds, hard seeds removed

steps: Wash the bitter gourd and lightly scrape the rough ridges with a knife or peeler. Cut into thin rounds; if the seeds are hard and red-tinged, push them out and discard them.
Rub the slices with a generous sprinkle of the salt and the turmeric and leave for 20-30 minutes. Then squeeze them firmly by the handful and throw away the bitter juice.

Heat most of the oil in a wide pan on medium heat. Add the bitter gourd slices, spread them out and fry uncovered for 8-10 minutes, turning every few minutes, until tender and golden at the edges. Lift them out onto a plate, leaving the oil behind.
In the same pan (add the rest of the oil if it looks dry), cook the onion and green chilli on medium heat for 6-8 minutes, stirring often, until the onion is soft and golden brown.
Turn the heat to low, add the red chilli powder, coriander powder and fennel powder and stir for 1 minute so the spices cook without burning.

Return the fried bitter gourd to the pan, add the amchur and the sugar or jaggery if using, and toss on medium heat for 2-3 minutes until coated and the edges crisp up again. Taste before adding any more salt, since the slices were salted earlier.
tips: Salting and squeezing out the juice is what tames the bitterness; do not skip it, and squeeze hard.
Taste before salting again at the end; the salting step leaves plenty behind.
Keep the slices thin and the pan uncovered so they crisp up rather than steam soft.

name: Keerai Masiyal
servesWith: hot rice with a spoon of ghee, alongside sambar or rasam

ingredients.prep: leaves and tender stems picked, washed well, roughly chopped

steps: Pick the spinach leaves and tender stems, discarding thick stems and yellowed leaves. Wash in 2-3 changes of water until no grit settles at the bottom of the bowl, drain and chop roughly.

Put the spinach in a pan with the green chilli, garlic, cumin seeds and a splash of water (the water clinging to the leaves is nearly enough). Cover and cook on medium for 4-5 minutes, until the leaves are fully wilted and soft but still green.
Let it cool for a few minutes, then mash with a wooden masher (mathu) or pulse 2-3 times in a mixer to a coarse mash - not a smooth puree. Mix in the salt.
Heat the oil in a small pan on medium. Splutter the mustard seeds, fry the urad dal until golden, then add the dried red chilli and asafoetida for 10 seconds.
Pour the tempering over the mashed spinach, mix, and warm through on low for a minute before serving.
tips: Salt only after mashing - spinach shrinks to a fraction of its volume and is very easy to over-salt.
Don't overcook the leaves; past 5-6 minutes they turn dull olive and taste flat.

name: Lauki Chana Dal

ingredients.prep: peeled, large seeds removed, cut into 1-inch cubes

steps: Rinse the chana dal 2-3 times and soak it in water for at least 30 minutes (1 hour is better). Drain before cooking.
Peel the bottle gourd and taste a small raw piece; if it is bitter, throw the whole gourd away. Scoop out large seeds and cut it into 1-inch cubes.

Heat the oil in a pressure cooker on medium heat. Add the cumin seeds and asafoetida; when the cumin crackles, add the onion and fry for 4-5 minutes until light golden. Add the ginger, garlic and green chilli and saute for 1 minute.
Add the tomato, turmeric powder, kashmiri red chilli powder, coriander powder and salt. Cook for 4-5 minutes, stirring, until the tomato is soft and oil separates.
Add the drained chana dal and the bottle gourd and stir for 1-2 minutes to coat. Pour in the water.

Close the lid and pressure-cook on medium heat for 4 whistles (3 if the dal was soaked for a full hour). Let the pressure release on its own, then check that a grain of dal crushes easily between your fingers; if not, cook 1 more whistle.
Open, stir in the garam masala and simmer for 2-3 minutes, adding hot water only if it is too thick. Garnish with coriander leaves and serve hot.
tips: Always taste a raw piece of bottle gourd first; a bitter one can make you ill, so discard it rather than cooking it.
Soak the chana dal ahead; unsoaked, it stays hard by the time the lauki has turned to mush.
Lauki releases water as it cooks, so use less water than you would for plain dal and adjust at the end.

name: Lauki ki Sabzi

ingredients.prep: peeled, hard seeds scooped out if any, cut into 1/2-inch cubes

steps: Peel the bottle gourd and cut off a thin slice from the stem end. Taste a tiny raw piece: if it is bitter at all, throw away the whole gourd and do not cook it.
Halve it lengthwise, scoop out the seeds if they are large and hard, and cut into 1/2-inch cubes.
Heat the oil in a kadhai on medium. Add the cumin seeds and hing and let the cumin crackle for a few seconds. Add the ginger and green chilli and saute for 30 seconds.
Add the tomato, turmeric, red chilli powder, coriander powder and salt. Cook 3-4 minutes, pressing with the spoon, until the tomato is soft and mushy.
Add the bottle gourd and stir well. Cover and cook on low for 12-15 minutes without adding water, stirring every 4-5 minutes, until the cubes turn translucent and soft but still hold their shape.
If there is a lot of liquid in the pan, uncover and cook on medium for 2-3 minutes to reduce it to a light coating.
Stir in the garam masala if using, scatter the coriander leaves and serve hot.
tips: Never cook or eat a bottle gourd that tastes bitter raw; bitter lauki can cause serious stomach poisoning, so always taste a sliver first.
Pick a young lauki that is light green, firm and whose skin dents with a fingernail; old ones have hard seeds and a spongy core.
No water is needed: lauki is mostly water. In a pressure cooker, 1 whistle on medium is enough; more turns it to mush.

name: Leek and Potato Soup

ingredients.prep: white and light green parts only, halved lengthwise, washed and thinly sliced

steps: Cut off the roots and the tough dark green tops of the leeks. Halve them lengthwise and rinse under running water, fanning the layers apart to wash out all the grit, then slice thinly.
Peel the potatoes and cut into 1/2-inch cubes; finely chop the onion and garlic.

Melt the butter in a heavy pot on medium-low heat. Add the leeks and onion with a little of the salt and cook for 8-10 minutes, stirring now and then, until very soft and translucent; do not let them brown.

Add the garlic and stir for 1 minute. Add the potatoes, the bay leaf if using and the stock or water. Bring to a boil, then cover and simmer on low heat for 15-20 minutes, until a potato cube breaks easily when pressed with a spoon.
Remove the bay leaf. Let the soup cool for a few minutes, then blend until smooth with a hand blender, or in a mixer in batches with the lid vented, since hot soup expands.

Return the soup to the pot, stir in the milk and heat gently on low heat without letting it boil hard. If it is too thick, add a little hot water until it coats the back of a spoon. Season with salt and pepper.
Serve hot, with a swirl of the cream if using.
tips: Wash the leeks after halving them; soil hides between the layers and a gritty soup cannot be fixed.
Cook the leeks gently until soft without colour; browned leeks turn the soup a muddy beige-brown and slightly bitter instead of pale and sweet.
Blend just until smooth; running potatoes too long in a high-speed mixer makes the soup gluey.

name: Matar Paneer

ingredients.prep: shelled fresh peas or frozen peas (buy about double this weight in the pod)

steps: Cut the paneer into 1-inch cubes and soak them in hot water for 10 minutes so they stay soft; drain before adding.
Heat the oil in a kadai on medium heat. Add the cumin seeds and bay leaf; when the cumin sizzles, add the onion and fry for 6-8 minutes until golden brown.
Add the ginger, garlic and green chilli and saute for 1 minute until the raw smell goes.
Lower the heat, add the turmeric powder, kashmiri red chilli powder and coriander powder and stir for 20-30 seconds. Immediately add the tomato puree and salt.
Cook on medium heat for 7-8 minutes, stirring often, until the masala thickens, darkens and oil separates at the edges.
Add the peas and stir for a minute, then pour in the water. Cover and simmer on low-medium heat for 8-10 minutes until fresh peas are tender (4-5 minutes is enough for frozen peas).
Add the drained paneer, garam masala and crushed kasuri methi. Simmer uncovered for 3-4 minutes so the paneer takes on the gravy; add a splash of hot water if it gets too thick.
Garnish with coriander leaves and serve hot.
tips: Cook the onion-tomato masala until the oil separates before any water goes in; an undercooked masala makes the gravy taste raw and sour.
Frozen peas need only a few minutes; overcooking makes them wrinkled and grey.
Soaking the paneer in hot water keeps it soft even if it was straight from the fridge.

name: Matar Pulao
steps: Rinse the basmati rice in 3-4 changes of water, soak it for 20-30 minutes, then drain it well.

Heat the ghee in a heavy-bottomed pot on medium heat. Add the cumin seeds, bay leaf, cinnamon, cloves, cardamom and the peppercorns if using, and let them sizzle for about 30 seconds until the cumin darkens slightly.
Add the onion and fry, stirring, for 5-6 minutes until evenly light golden brown.
Add the green chilli and peas and saute for 2 minutes.
Add the drained rice and stir very gently on low-medium heat for 1-2 minutes so every grain is coated in ghee without breaking.
Pour in the water, add salt and bring to a boil on high heat. Boil uncovered for 4-5 minutes until the water drops to the level of the rice and small holes appear on the surface.
Turn the heat to the lowest setting, cover tightly and cook for 12-15 minutes without opening.
Switch off the heat, keep covered for 10 minutes, then fluff gently with a fork and serve.
tips: Fry the onion to an even light golden brown; pale onion adds no flavour and dark brown onion turns the pulao bitter.
Frying the soaked rice gently in ghee before adding the water coats the grains and helps them stay separate; stir softly so they do not break.
Do not stir after covering, and let it rest before fluffing, or the grains break.

name: Mix Veg Sabzi
steps: Cut all the vegetables small and even, keeping the potato and carrot the smallest because they take the longest to cook.

Heat the oil in a kadai on medium heat. Add the cumin seeds and let them splutter for 20 seconds. Add the onion and saute for 4-5 minutes until light golden, then add the ginger and green chilli and stir for 30 seconds.

Turn the heat to low, add the turmeric, red chilli powder and coriander powder and stir for 15 seconds. Add the tomato with a pinch of the salt and cook for 3-4 minutes until soft and the oil starts to separate.

Add the potato and carrot with the rest of the salt and stir on medium heat for 1 minute. Sprinkle 1 tablespoon of water, cover and cook on low heat for 5 minutes, until the potato is starting to soften at the edges. Then add the beans, cauliflower and fresh peas and toss to coat.

Sprinkle 1-2 more tablespoons of water, cover and cook on low heat for 8-10 minutes, stirring every 3-4 minutes, until the potato and carrot are tender, the cauliflower is just tender but holding its shape, and the beans are cooked through but still green. If using frozen peas, add them for the last 5 minutes.
Uncover and cook on medium heat for 2-3 minutes, stirring, until the sabzi is dry.
Add the garam masala and, if using, crush the kasuri methi between your palms over the pan; toss well and finish with the coriander leaves.
tips: Potato and carrot are the slowest to soften, so cut them smallest and give them their 5-minute head start; added together with the cauliflower, the cauliflower turns to mush before the carrot is tender.
Keep the water to a sprinkle and dry it off at the end; this is a dry sabzi, not a curry.

name: Mooli Paratha

ingredients.item: water (only if the dough needs it)

steps: Mix the grated radish with some of the salt and leave it for 10-15 minutes to release its water.
Squeeze the radish in fistfuls as hard as you can over a bowl, and keep the radish water.

Add the radish water to the atta a little at a time and knead into a soft, smooth dough. Stop once the dough comes together; you may not need all of it. If it is still stiff, add a few drops of plain water. The radish water is already salted, so taste before adding more salt. Cover and rest for 20 minutes.

Mix the squeezed radish with the green chilli, ginger, coriander leaves, ajwain and red chilli powder, plus the amchur if using. Taste and add salt only if needed. If the filling turns wet while standing, squeeze it again just before stuffing.
Divide the dough into balls (2 per serving). Roll one into a 4-inch disc with thinner edges, put a portion of filling in the centre, gather the edges over it, pinch to seal and flatten gently.
Dust with atta and roll gently into a 6-7 inch paratha, patching any tear with a pinch of dry atta.
Heat a tawa on medium-high, then turn it to medium. Cook the paratha for 30-40 seconds until bubbles appear, then flip.
Spread ghee on both sides one at a time, pressing the edges with a spatula, and cook for about 1 minute per side until golden-brown spots appear on both sides. Serve hot.
tips: Squeeze the grated radish really hard; mooli holds a lot of water and a wet filling tears the paratha.
Knead the dough with the squeezed-out radish water instead of plain water so its flavour goes into the paratha, but add it gradually; a slack dough tears when stuffed.

Salt the radish with about 1/8 tsp per serving (1/2 tsp for four); a mere pinch draws out too little water and the filling keeps weeping. That salt carries into the dough and filling, so taste before salting either again.

name: Mooli ki Sabzi

ingredients.prep: peeled and cut into 1/4-inch dice or coarsely grated (the weight is the root alone); if it came with fresh leaves, wash and finely chop them too and add them on top of this weight

steps: Peel the radish and cut it into small 1/4-inch dice, or grate it coarsely. If the radish came with fresh green leaves, wash them in two changes of water, discard yellow or tough stems, and chop finely.

Heat the oil in a kadhai on medium (if using mustard oil, heat it on high until it just smokes, then lower the heat to medium and wait 30 seconds). Add the cumin seeds, ajwain (if using) and hing and let them crackle for about 10 seconds.
Add the ginger and green chilli and saute for 30 seconds.
Add the turmeric, red chilli powder and coriander powder, stir for 10 seconds, then immediately add the radish (and the chopped leaves) with the salt. Toss well.
Cover and cook on low for 10-12 minutes, stirring once or twice, until the radish turns translucent and soft. Do not add water; the salt draws plenty out of the radish.
Uncover, raise the heat to medium and cook 5-7 minutes, stirring often, until all the released water has evaporated and the sabzi is dry.
Sprinkle the amchur, stir for 1 minute and serve hot.
tips: Choose firm, heavy radishes that snap cleanly; light, spongy ones are pithy inside and turn stringy.
The sharp raw-radish smell is normal while it cooks and mellows completely once the water dries off, so do not stop early while it is still wet.
Leaves make it tastier; if you have them, add roughly one part chopped leaves to two parts radish, on top of the radish weight.

name: Mushroom Masala

ingredients.prep: wiped clean, stem ends trimmed, quartered or thickly sliced

steps: Clean the mushrooms by wiping them with a damp cloth or giving them a quick rinse in a colander; drain well and pat dry. Trim the stem ends and quarter or slice them.
Heat the oil in a kadai on medium-high heat. Add the cumin seeds; when they crackle, add the onion and fry for 6-7 minutes until golden.
Add the ginger, garlic and green chilli and saute for 1 minute.
Add the tomato, turmeric powder, kashmiri red chilli powder, coriander powder and salt. Cook on medium heat for 5-6 minutes until the tomato is mushy and oil separates.
Turn the heat to high, add the mushrooms and stir-fry for 4-5 minutes. They will release water; keep cooking until most of it has evaporated.
Add the water, garam masala and crushed kasuri methi. Simmer uncovered on medium heat for 4-5 minutes until the mushrooms are tender and the gravy thickly coats them.
Garnish with coriander leaves and serve hot.
tips: Never soak mushrooms in water; they soak it up and turn soggy.
Cook the mushrooms on high heat so their liquid boils off quickly; on low heat they stew in it and turn soggy and slimy.
Mushrooms add their own water, so add the extra water only after they have cooked down.

name: Mushroom Matar

ingredients.prep: wiped clean, stem ends trimmed, sliced
shelled fresh peas or frozen peas (buy about double this weight in the pod)

steps: Heat the oil in a kadai on medium heat. Add the cumin seeds and bay leaf; when the cumin sizzles, add the onion and fry for 6-7 minutes until golden.
Add the ginger, garlic and green chilli and saute for 1 minute until the raw smell goes.

Add the turmeric powder, kashmiri red chilli powder and coriander powder, stir for 20 seconds, then add the tomato puree and salt. Cook for 6-7 minutes, stirring, until the masala thickens and oil separates.
If using fresh peas, add them now with the water, cover and simmer on low-medium heat for 6-8 minutes until nearly tender. (Frozen peas go in with the mushrooms in the next step, with the water.)
Add the mushrooms, turn the heat to medium-high and cook uncovered for 6-7 minutes, stirring, until the mushrooms are cooked through and the gravy thickens again.
Stir in the garam masala and crushed kasuri methi and simmer for 1 minute. Add a splash of hot water if you want a looser gravy.
Garnish with coriander leaves and serve hot.
tips: Fresh peas take longer than mushrooms, so give the peas a head start in the gravy before the mushrooms go in.
Do not cover the pan after adding the mushrooms; trapped steam makes the gravy watery and the mushrooms limp.

name: Onion Pakoda
servesWith: hot masala chai and green chutney

ingredients.prep: halved and thinly sliced into half-moons, layers separated

steps: Peel the onions, halve them and slice into thin half-moons. Separate the layers with your fingers so no slices stay stuck together.

Put the onions in a bowl with the salt, green chilli, ginger, coriander leaves, torn curry leaves, ajwain, turmeric powder and red chilli powder. Mix well and leave for 10 minutes so the onions release their moisture.
Meanwhile, heat the oil for deep frying in a kadai on medium heat.

Add the besan and rice flour to the onions along with the hot oil taken from the kadai. Mix and squeeze with your fingers so the flour sticks to the onions using only their own moisture. Sprinkle water a teaspoon at a time only if the flour stays dry - the mixture should be thick and clumpy, never a pourable batter.
Test the oil by dropping in a small pinch of the mixture: it should sizzle at once and rise to the top in 2-3 seconds.
Drop small, loose clusters into the oil with your fingertips, without pressing them together and without crowding the kadai.
Fry on medium heat for 4-5 minutes, turning a couple of times, until deep golden and crisp and the bubbling around them has quietened.
Lift out with a slotted spoon, drain on a steel strainer or paper towel, and fry the rest in batches. Serve hot.
tips: Never add water before the onions have rested; a wet mixture soaks up oil and gives soggy pakodas.
Fry on medium, not high - high heat browns the outside while the besan inside stays raw.
Drop loose, craggy clusters rather than tight balls; the thin edges are what turn crisp.

name: Onion Tomato Chutney
