steps: Heat most of the oil in a pan on medium heat. Add most of the urad dal and fry for about 1 minute until golden, then add the dry red chillies and fry 20 seconds until they darken a shade.
Add the onion and garlic and saute for 4-5 minutes, until the onion is soft and translucent with light golden edges.
Add the tomatoes, tamarind and salt. Cook for 5-6 minutes, stirring, until the tomatoes are soft and mushy and the mixture looks thick.
Turn off the heat and let it cool completely.
Grind to a smooth paste, adding a splash of water only if needed to get the blades moving.

For the tempering, heat the remaining oil on medium heat, add the mustard seeds and let them splutter, then add the remaining urad dal and fry 20-30 seconds until golden. Add the curry leaves and asafoetida and stir for 5 seconds until the leaves crackle.
Pour the tempering over the chutney, mix, and serve at room temperature.
tips: Saute the onion until properly soft and sweet - undercooked onion turns sharp and slightly bitter once ground.
Always cool before grinding; hot chutney in a sealed grinder jar can burst out when opened.
Use the tamarind only if the tomatoes are mild; with sour tomatoes, leave it out.

name: Palak Paneer

ingredients.prep: thick stems removed, washed well in 2-3 changes of water

steps: Bring a large pot of water to a rolling boil on high heat with a pinch of salt. Add the spinach and blanch for 1 to 2 minutes, only until the leaves wilt and turn bright green.

Drain the spinach and plunge it straight into a bowl of ice-cold water for 2 minutes to stop the cooking. Squeeze out lightly, then blend with the green chilli into a smooth puree, adding only 2-3 spoons of water.
Cut the paneer into 1-inch cubes and soak them in hot salted water for 10 minutes while you make the masala; drain before using.

Heat the ghee or oil in a kadai on medium heat. Add the cumin seeds; when they crackle, add the onion and fry for 5-6 minutes until light golden. Add the ginger and garlic and saute for 1 minute until the raw smell goes.
Add the tomato, turmeric powder, kashmiri red chilli powder, coriander powder and salt. Cook for 4-5 minutes, stirring, until the tomato turns mushy and oil begins to separate at the edges.
Turn the heat to low and add the spinach puree and the water for a thick, pourable gravy. Simmer for 3-4 minutes with a lid held half over the pan because it splutters, stirring now and then.
Add the paneer, garam masala and kasuri methi crushed between your palms. Simmer for 2 minutes, just until the paneer is heated through.
Switch off the heat, stir in the fresh cream if using, taste for salt and serve hot.
tips: Do not blanch the spinach longer than 2 minutes or boil the puree for long; overcooked spinach turns dull olive and slightly bitter.
The ice-water plunge right after blanching is what keeps the gravy bright green.
Add the paneer at the very end; boiling it in the gravy makes it rubbery.

name: Palak Paratha
steps: Wash the spinach in 2-3 changes of water to remove all grit and discard the thick stems.
Bring a pan of water to a boil, drop in the spinach and blanch for 1-2 minutes until just wilted and bright green. Lift it straight into cold water, then drain and squeeze lightly.
Blend the spinach with the green chilli, ginger and garlic into a smooth puree, adding no water or only a spoonful if the blender needs it.

In a bowl, mix the atta with the ajwain (crushed between your palms), cumin powder, salt, the oil for the dough and the red chilli powder if using. Add the puree a little at a time and knead into a soft, smooth dough, adding a few drops of water or a little atta only if needed. Cover and rest for 20 minutes.
Divide the dough into balls (2 per serving). Roll one into a 5-inch disc, brush a little oil over it, dust with atta, fold it in half and then in half again into a triangle.
Dust with atta and roll the triangle out evenly to about 7 inches along each side.
Heat a tawa on medium-high, then turn it to medium. Cook the paratha for 30-40 seconds until bubbles appear, then flip and cook for 30 seconds more.
Brush oil on both sides one at a time, pressing gently with a spatula, and cook for about 1 minute per side until light golden-brown spots appear and the layers puff. Serve hot.
tips: Blanch for no more than 2 minutes and cool in cold water immediately; overcooked spinach turns the parathas dull olive and slightly bitter.
Add the puree gradually, because the amount of liquid in spinach varies and too much makes a sticky dough.
Cook on medium, not high; high heat browns the parathas before they cook through and hides the green colour.

name: Palakura Pappu
servesWith: hot rice with a vegetable fry

ingredients.prep: leaves and tender stems, washed well and chopped

steps: Rinse the toor dal 2-3 times, then pressure cook it with the water, turmeric powder and a few drops of the oil on medium heat for 4 whistles. Let the pressure drop on its own.
While the dal cooks, wash the spinach in 2-3 changes of water until no grit settles at the bottom of the bowl, drain and chop it. If using tamarind, soak it in just enough warm water to cover it.

While the cooker's pressure drops, heat the remaining oil in a pan on medium. Add the mustard seeds and, once they splutter, the cumin seeds, dry red chilli and garlic; fry until the garlic is golden. Add the curry leaves and asafoetida.
Add the onion and green chillies and saute for about 3 minutes until soft. Add the tomato and cook for 3-4 minutes until it turns soft and pulpy.
Add the spinach and cook uncovered on medium for 3-4 minutes, stirring, until it has fully wilted and most of the water it releases has cooked off.

Open the cooker, mash the dal smooth and tip it into the pan with the salt and the squeezed tamarind pulp if using. Simmer on low for 4-5 minutes, stirring, adding hot water if needed until the dal is thick but pourable. Serve hot.
tips: Wash the spinach before you chop it and in several changes of water; grit in a finished dal cannot be fixed.
Keep the final simmer short once the dal goes in; long boiling turns the spinach dull and dark.

name: Paneer Butter Masala
servesWith: butter naan, roti or jeera rice
steps: Heat the oil with a little of the butter in a pan on medium heat. Add the onion, ginger, garlic and green chilli and saute for 3-4 minutes until the onion is soft and translucent but not browned.
Add the tomato, cashews, salt and a splash of the water. Cover and cook on medium heat for 8-10 minutes until the tomatoes are completely mushy and the cashews are soft.
Let it cool for 5-10 minutes, then blend to a very smooth puree. For a silky restaurant-style gravy, push it through a sieve.
Melt most of the remaining butter in the same pan on low heat. Add the kashmiri red chilli powder and stir for 10 seconds without letting it darken, then pour in the puree.
Cook on low-medium heat for 5-6 minutes, stirring, until the gravy thickens and butter starts to shine on the surface.
Add the rest of the water to get a thick but flowing gravy, then the sugar and garam masala. Simmer for 2-3 minutes; taste and adjust salt and sugar.
Add the paneer cubes and kasuri methi crushed between your palms. Simmer for 2 minutes, only until the paneer is heated through.
Turn the heat to the lowest, stir in the fresh cream and switch off. Finish with the last bit of butter on top and serve hot.
tips: Do not brown the onion; cooking it only until soft keeps the gravy bright orange and mildly sweet.
Blend the tomato-cashew mixture until completely smooth, and sieve it if you can; a grainy gravy is the most common complaint with this dish.
Add the cream on the lowest heat and do not boil it afterwards, or it can split against the tomato's acidity.

name: Parangikai Kootu
steps: Rinse the moong dal and cook it with the turmeric powder and about three times its volume of water - 2-3 whistles in a pressure cooker, or about 20 minutes in an open pot - until soft and mashable. Mash it lightly.
Grind the grated coconut, cumin seeds and green chilli to a smooth paste with a little water.
Put the pumpkin in a pot with salt, the jaggery if using, and just enough water to half-cover it. Cover and cook on medium for 6-8 minutes until the pumpkin is fork-tender but still holds its shape.

Add the cooked dal and the coconut paste and stir gently, adding a little hot water if needed for a thick, spoonable consistency. Simmer on low for 3-4 minutes until the raw coconut smell is gone - do not boil it hard.
For the tempering, heat the coconut oil in a small pan on medium. Splutter the mustard seeds, fry the urad dal until golden, then add the dried red chilli, curry leaves and asafoetida for 10 seconds.
Pour the tempering over the kootu, mix and serve warm.
tips: Check the pumpkin at 6 minutes - it goes from tender to dissolved very quickly.
Kootu should hold on a spoon, not run like sambar; it thickens further as it cools, so loosen with hot water when reheating.

name: Aloo Tamatar ki Sabzi

ingredients.prep: peeled and cut into 1-inch cubes, kept in water

steps: Peel the potatoes, cut them into 1-inch cubes and keep them in a bowl of water. Chop the tomatoes finely or puree them.

Heat the oil on medium in a pressure cooker big enough to stay no more than two-thirds full once the potatoes and water go in (a 3-litre cooker for up to 4 servings, 5 litres for up to 8). Add the cumin seeds and hing and let the cumin crackle. Add the ginger and green chilli and saute for 30 seconds.

Add the turmeric, Kashmiri red chilli powder and coriander powder, stir for 10 seconds, then add the tomatoes and salt. Cook 5-6 minutes, mashing with the spoon, until the tomatoes break down into a thick pulp and oil shows at the edges.
Drain the potatoes, add them to the cooker and stir for 1-2 minutes to coat them in the masala. Pour in the water and stir.
Close the lid and pressure cook on medium heat for 2 whistles (about 8-10 minutes). Turn off the heat and let the pressure drop on its own.

Open the cooker and crush a few of the potato cubes (roughly one in five) against the side to thicken the gravy. Simmer uncovered for 2-3 minutes; add a little hot water if it is too thick. It should be a pouring gravy, not a paste.
Crush the kasuri methi (if using) between your palms and add it with the garam masala. Simmer 1 minute, scatter the coriander leaves and serve hot.
tips: Crushing a few potatoes is what thickens this gravy; there is no need for onion, cream or flour.
Use ripe red tomatoes. If they are very sour, add a pinch of sugar at the end.

No pressure cooker? Boil the potato cubes separately in lightly salted water for 10-12 minutes until just tender, drain, then add them to the cooked tomato masala with the water and simmer covered for 8-10 minutes. Raw potato simmered straight in the tomato gravy can take 30 minutes or more, because the tomato's acid keeps it firm.

name: Sarson ka Saag
servesWith: makki di roti with white butter and jaggery

ingredients.prep: tough lower stems discarded, tender stems peeled, leaves and stems roughly chopped

steps: Wash the chopped mustard greens and spinach in a large bowl of water, lifting the leaves out each time, in 3-4 changes of water until no grit settles at the bottom.

Put the greens in a pressure cooker with half the ginger, half the garlic, the green chilli, salt and the water. Pressure-cook on medium heat for 4-5 whistles (about 15 minutes) until the mustard stems are completely soft. Let the pressure release on its own.
Cool slightly, then pulse the greens with their liquid into a coarse paste in a blender, or mash them with a wooden masher. Do not make it a smooth puree.
Return the saag to the pan on low heat. Whisk the makki ka atta with a few spoons of water into a lump-free slurry and stir it in.
Cook on low heat for 15-20 minutes, partly covered because it splutters, stirring every few minutes, until the raw flour taste is gone and the saag is thick and glossy.

For the tadka, heat the ghee in a small pan on medium heat. Add the onion and fry for 5-6 minutes until golden brown, then add the remaining ginger and garlic and fry for 1 minute until the garlic is light golden. Switch off the heat and stir in the kashmiri red chilli powder if using.
Pour the tadka into the saag, mix well and simmer for 5 minutes. Taste for salt.
Serve hot with a spoonful of white butter or ghee on top.
tips: Use roughly two parts mustard greens to one part spinach; mustard alone is sharp and bitter, and spinach mellows it.
Cook the saag on low for the full time after adding the makki ka atta; undercooked, it tastes raw and gritty.
Sarson ka saag tastes even better the next day; it keeps in the fridge for 2-3 days.

name: Garlic Butter Sauteed Asparagus
servesWith: a bowl of soup, pasta or garlic bread

ingredients.prep: woody ends snapped off; lower third peeled if the spears are thick

steps: Rinse the asparagus. Bend each spear near its base; it snaps where the woody part ends, so discard the ends. If the spears are thick (about 1 cm across or more), peel the lower third; thin and medium spears need no peeling. Pat dry and finely chop the garlic.
Heat the oil and butter in a wide pan on medium heat until the butter melts and foams.

Add the asparagus in a single layer and cook for 4-5 minutes, rolling the spears now and then, until bright green with a few browned spots and a knife slides into the thick end with slight resistance. Thin spears need about 3 minutes, very thick ones 6-7.
Lower the heat to medium-low, add the garlic and chilli flakes if using, and stir for 30-45 seconds until the garlic is fragrant and pale golden, spooning the garlic butter over the spears.
Season with salt and pepper, turn off the heat and squeeze over the lemon juice if using. Serve immediately.
tips: Add the garlic only at the end; left in butter for the whole cook it burns and turns bitter.
Buy firm spears with tight, closed tips; limp asparagus does not recover in the pan.
Use a pan wide enough to hold the spears in one layer, or they steam and go limp instead of browning.

name: Shalgam ki Sabzi
steps: Peel the turnips, cutting away any fibrous patch near the root end, and cut them into 1/2-inch cubes.

Heat the oil in a kadhai on medium (if using mustard oil, heat it on high until it just starts to smoke, then turn the heat to medium and wait 30 seconds). Add the cumin seeds and hing; let the cumin crackle for a few seconds.
Add the onion and saute on medium for 5-6 minutes until golden. Add the ginger, garlic and green chilli and saute 1 minute until the raw smell goes.

Add the turmeric, red chilli powder and coriander powder with a splash of water and stir for 30 seconds. Add the tomato and salt and cook 4-5 minutes, stirring, until the tomato is soft and oil shows at the edges.

Add the turnip and toss to coat in the masala. Cover and cook on low for 15-20 minutes, stirring every 5 minutes, until a knife slides through a cube with no resistance. Add a splash of water only if the masala starts to stick; the turnip releases its own water.

Lightly press a few pieces with the back of the spoon so the sabzi holds together. Stir in the jaggery (if using) and the garam masala and cook uncovered on medium for 2-3 minutes until any liquid has dried off.
Turn off the heat, scatter the coriander leaves and serve hot.
tips: Buy small, firm, heavy turnips with smooth skin; large ones are woody and sharp-tasting.
A little jaggery (about 1/2 tsp per serving) is traditional in Punjabi homes: it rounds off the turnip's slight bitterness without making the dish sweet.
Cook covered on low and do not add water at the start, or the cubes turn watery and bland instead of absorbing the masala.

name: Sorakaya Kura

ingredients.prep: peeled, hard seeds removed, cut into 1/2-inch cubes

steps: Peel the bottle gourd and taste a small raw piece; if it is bitter, discard the whole gourd. Remove any hard seeds and cut the rest into 1/2-inch cubes.
Heat the oil in a pan on medium. Add the mustard seeds and, once they splutter, the cumin seeds, chana dal and urad dal; fry until the dals turn golden, then add the curry leaves.
Add the onion and green chillies and saute for about 3 minutes until soft. Add the tomato and cook for 3-4 minutes until soft and pulpy.

Add the bottle gourd, turmeric powder, red chilli powder, coriander powder and salt and mix well. Cover and cook on low for 10-12 minutes, stirring once or twice, until the cubes turn translucent and are tender when pressed; the gourd releases its own water, so add none.
Uncover and cook on medium for 2-3 minutes until the juices reduce to a light gravy that coats the pieces. Scatter the coriander leaves over and serve.
tips: Never cook a bottle gourd that tastes bitter raw; a bitter bottle gourd carries natural toxins (cucurbitacins) that can cause serious stomach illness, so discard the whole gourd.
Do not add water at the start; bottle gourd is mostly water and the curry turns thin and bland.
Choose a young, pale-green gourd with glossy skin that a fingernail pierces easily; old ones are fibrous and seedy.

name: Shakarkandi Chaat
servesWith: on its own as an evening snack

ingredients.prep: scrubbed, cooked whole in the skin, then peeled and cubed

steps: Scrub the sweet potatoes well under running water and keep them whole, with the skin on.

Cook them: pressure cook with about a cup of water for 2 whistles on medium heat (3 whistles for thick ones), or roast in an oven at 200°C for 35-40 minutes - the oven route takes about 25 minutes longer than the cooker. They are done when a knife goes in with just a little resistance - cooked through but not mushy.
Let them cool for 5 minutes, peel, and cut into three-quarter-inch cubes.
For a roasted street flavour (optional), heat the oil in a pan on medium-high heat and toss the cubes for 3-4 minutes until the edges turn golden in spots.
In a bowl, toss the cubes with the chaat masala, roasted cumin powder, black salt, red chilli powder, green chilli and lemon juice until evenly coated.
Taste, and add plain salt only if needed. Top with coriander leaves, pomegranate arils and a drizzle of sweet tamarind chutney, and serve warm straight away.
tips: Stop cooking while the sweet potato still has a slight bite; overcooked cubes turn to paste when tossed.
Chaat masala and black salt are both salty - taste before adding any plain salt.
Choose slender sweet potatoes of even thickness so they cook evenly.

name: Tomato Chutney
steps: Heat most of the oil in a pan on medium heat. Add the chana dal and most of the urad dal and fry, stirring, for 1-2 minutes until golden and nutty-smelling.
Add the dry red chillies and garlic and fry for 30 seconds until the chillies puff slightly and darken a shade - do not let them blacken.

Add the tomatoes, salt and tamarind. Cook on medium heat for 7-8 minutes, stirring now and then, until the tomatoes are completely soft and mushy, the raw smell has gone and the mixture has thickened.
Turn off the heat and let it cool completely.
Grind to a smooth or slightly coarse paste. The tomatoes carry enough moisture, so add water only a teaspoon at a time if the blades will not turn.

For the tempering, heat the remaining oil on medium heat, add the mustard seeds and let them splutter, then add the remaining urad dal and fry 20-30 seconds until golden. Add the curry leaves and asafoetida and stir for 5 seconds until the leaves crackle.
Pour the tempering over the chutney, mix, and taste for salt.
tips: Cook the tomatoes until really mushy and thick - undercooked tomato gives a raw, sour, watery chutney.
Control the heat with the number of dry red chillies; Byadgi or Kashmiri chillies give colour with less heat.
Keeps for 2 days in the fridge in a clean, dry container.

name: Tomato Pappu
steps: Rinse the toor dal 2-3 times until the water runs nearly clear; soak it for 20 minutes if you have the time. If using tamarind, soak it in just enough warm water to cover it.

Put the dal, water, tomatoes, onion, green chillies, turmeric powder and a few drops of the oil into a pressure cooker. Cook on medium heat for 4 whistles, then let the pressure drop on its own, about 10 minutes.
Open the cooker and check that the dal crushes completely between your fingers; if not, give it one more whistle. Mash the dal and tomatoes with a ladle or whisk into one smooth, thick mass.

Stir in the salt, the red chilli powder if using and, if your tomatoes are mild, the squeezed tamarind pulp. Simmer on low for 3-4 minutes, stirring, adding hot water if needed until it is thick but pourable.

For the tempering, heat the remaining oil in a small pan on medium. Add the mustard seeds and, once they splutter, the cumin seeds, dry red chilli and garlic; fry until the garlic is golden, about 30 seconds. Turn off the heat and stir in the curry leaves and asafoetida.
Pour the tempering over the dal, add the coriander leaves, stir and serve hot.
tips: Use ripe, sour country (naatu) tomatoes for the tang; the tamarind is only needed when your tomatoes are mild.
The pappu thickens as it stands; loosen it with hot water before serving and check the salt again.

name: Tomato Rasam
servesWith: hot rice with ghee, or sipped warm from a cup
steps: Soak the tamarind in hot water - about 1/4 cup per serving - for 10 minutes, then squeeze and strain it, keeping the tamarind water.
Coarsely pound the black pepper, cumin seeds and garlic in a mortar (or pulse 2-3 times in a dry mixer jar) - aim for a rough crush, not a fine powder.

Put the tomato in a pot with the tamarind water, turmeric powder, salt, half the curry leaves and about half a cup of water per serving. Boil on medium for 8-10 minutes until the tomatoes are completely soft and the raw tamarind smell has gone, then mash the tomatoes against the side of the pot with a ladle.

Add the pounded pepper-cumin-garlic, the asafoetida and another half cup of water per serving. Lower the heat to medium-low and heat without stirring for 3-4 minutes, until a layer of froth rises to the top and just starts to break at the edges. Switch off at once - do not let it boil.
In a small pan, heat the ghee on medium, add the mustard seeds and let them splutter, then add the dried red chilli and the remaining curry leaves for a few seconds.
Pour the tempering over the rasam, add the coriander leaves and keep it covered for 5 minutes so the aroma stays in before serving.
tips: Never let rasam boil hard after the pepper and cumin go in - switch off at the first froth, or it turns bitter and loses its aroma.
Use ripe red tomatoes; if yours are very sour, use less tamarind.
For a vegan rasam, temper in oil instead of ghee.

name: Tomato Rice
servesWith: potato fry, papad or onion raita
steps: Rinse the rice and cook it with the water (3 whistles on medium in a pressure cooker, or bring it to a boil in a covered pot, then cook on low for 15-18 minutes until the water is absorbed) until soft but still separate. Spread it on a wide plate to cool until just warm.

Heat the oil in a kadai on medium heat and add the mustard seeds. When they crackle, add the chana dal and fry for about 20 seconds, then add the urad dal and the cashews if using and fry for about 40 seconds more until the dals and cashews turn golden. Add the asafoetida and curry leaves.
Add the onion and green chilli and saute for 3-4 minutes until the onion is soft and just turning golden.
Add the ginger and garlic and saute for 1 minute until the raw smell goes.
Add the tomato, turmeric powder and salt. Cover and cook on medium for 6-8 minutes, stirring now and then, until the tomato breaks down completely and mashes easily under the spoon.
Add the red chilli powder, and the garam masala if using, and cook uncovered for 3-4 minutes, stirring, until the masala is thick and jammy and oil shows at the edges.
Turn the heat to low, add the cooled rice and fold it in gently with a flat spatula for 2 minutes until every grain is evenly coated. Taste and adjust salt.
Scatter the coriander leaves over the rice, cover and rest for 5 minutes before serving.
tips: Cook the tomatoes until the oil separates; undercooked tomato masala makes the rice sour and wet.
Use rice that has cooled down; hot, freshly cooked rice breaks and turns mushy when mixed.
If your tomatoes are very sour, a small pinch of sugar in the masala balances them.

name: Tomato Soup
servesWith: garlic bread or hot buttered toast
steps: Heat the butter in a heavy-bottomed pan (or a pressure cooker) on medium heat, keeping a little aside if making croutons. Add the bay leaf, then the onion and garlic, and saute 2-3 minutes until the onion is soft and translucent - do not let it brown.
Add the carrot and tomatoes with a little salt. Cook on medium for 4-5 minutes, stirring, until the tomatoes soften and release their juice.

Pour in the water, cover and simmer on low-medium heat for 15 minutes (or pressure cook for 2 whistles on medium), until the tomatoes have collapsed and the carrot crushes easily against the side of the pan.

While the soup simmers, if making croutons, cut the bread into small cubes and toast them in the butter kept aside, in a separate pan on low-medium heat, stirring, for 4-5 minutes until golden and crisp. Set aside.
Take the soup off the heat, remove the bay leaf and let it cool for 5-10 minutes. Blend to a completely smooth puree.
Pour the puree through a fine sieve back into the pan, pressing the pulp with the back of a spoon. Discard the skins and seeds left in the sieve.

Bring the soup back to a gentle simmer on low heat and stir in the sugar and black pepper powder. For a thicker soup, mix the cornflour with a little cold water, stir it in and simmer 2 minutes until the soup lightly coats the spoon.
Taste and adjust salt. Turn off the heat and stir in the cream. Serve hot with a swirl of cream and the croutons, if made, on top.
tips: Use fully ripe, deep-red tomatoes. If the soup still tastes sharp, add sugar a pinch at a time rather than all at once.
Do not skip straining - it is what gives the smooth, velvety restaurant texture.
Add the cream off the heat and do not boil the soup again after it goes in, or it can split.

name: Turai ki Sabzi

ingredients.prep: hard ridges scraped off, cut into 1/2-inch pieces

steps: Wash the ridge gourd, trim both ends and scrape off only the hard ridges with a peeler, leaving the green skin between them. Taste a small piece from the stem end and discard the gourd if it is bitter. Cut into 1/2-inch pieces.
Heat the oil in a kadhai on medium. Add the cumin seeds and hing and let them crackle for a few seconds.
Add the onion and saute 3-4 minutes until soft and just turning golden at the edges. Add the ginger and green chilli and saute 30 seconds.
Add the turmeric, red chilli powder and coriander powder and stir for 20 seconds, then add the tomato and salt. Cook 3-4 minutes until the tomato is soft.
Add the ridge gourd and mix. Cover and cook on low for 8-10 minutes without adding water, stirring once, until the pieces are soft and translucent and have released their juices.
Uncover and cook on medium for 2-3 minutes to reduce the liquid to a light coating; leave it slightly juicy if you are eating it with rice.
Scatter the coriander leaves and serve hot.
tips: Buy slender, firm, bright-green ridge gourds that feel heavy for their size and whose ridges give slightly to a fingernail; limp, bendy ones are stale, and thick ones that feel light and spongy are over-mature, fibrous and full of hard seeds.
Do not add water and do not overcook: ridge gourd goes from tender to mush in a couple of minutes.
Leave some green skin between the ridges; it keeps the pieces from falling apart.

name: Vangi Bath

ingredients.prep: cut into thin 2-inch strips, kept in salted water

steps: Rinse the rice and cook it with the water (3 whistles on medium in a pressure cooker, or bring it to a boil in a covered pot, then cook on low for 15-18 minutes until the water is absorbed) until soft but still separate. Spread it on a wide plate to cool.

Heat the oil in a kadai on medium heat and add the mustard seeds. When they crackle, add the peanuts if using and fry for about 1 minute until they start to darken. Add the chana dal and fry for about 20 seconds, then add the urad dal and fry for about 40 seconds more until both dals turn golden and any peanuts are crisp. Add the asafoetida and curry leaves.

Drain the brinjal and add it with the turmeric powder and salt. Toss, cover and cook on low-medium heat for 6-8 minutes, stirring once or twice, until the brinjal is soft right through but still holds its shape.
Add the tamarind extract and jaggery and cook uncovered for 2 minutes until the raw tamarind smell is gone and the pan looks fairly dry.
Lower the heat, add the vangi bath powder and stir for 1 minute until fragrant and the brinjal is well coated. Do not let the powder scorch.
Add the cooled rice, and the grated dry coconut if using, and fold gently on low heat for 2 minutes until the rice is evenly coloured. Taste and add more salt or powder if needed.
Scatter the coriander leaves over the rice and serve warm.
tips: Pick small, glossy, tender brinjals with few seeds; large seedy ones turn bitter and mushy.
Keep the heat low once the vangi bath powder goes in; it contains roasted dals and chillies and burns within seconds.
Store-bought powders differ in heat, so start with the amount given and add more at the end after tasting.

name: Vankaya Tomato Kura

ingredients.prep: cut into 1-inch pieces, kept in salted water

steps: Cut the brinjals into 1-inch pieces and drop them straight into a bowl of salted water so they do not darken.
Heat the oil in a pan on medium. Add the mustard seeds and, once they splutter, the cumin seeds, chana dal and urad dal; fry until the dals turn golden, then add the curry leaves.
Add the onion and green chillies and saute for 3-4 minutes until soft and lightly golden.
Drain the brinjal and add it with the turmeric powder and salt. Toss, cover and cook on low for 6-8 minutes, stirring once, until the pieces start to soften at the edges.

Add the tomatoes, red chilli powder and coriander powder and mix. Cover and cook on low for 8-10 minutes, until the tomatoes collapse and the brinjal is soft all the way through; press a few tomato pieces against the pan to thicken the gravy. Add a splash of water only if it starts to stick.
Uncover and cook for 1-2 minutes until the gravy thickens and oil shows at the edges. Scatter the coriander leaves over and serve.
tips: Use small, tender brinjals (purple or green); large ones are seedy and stay spongy.
Hold back the water; brinjal and tomato release plenty, and added water makes a thin, washed-out curry.
Check a piece of brinjal before serving; undercooked brinjal is squeaky and spongy, so give it a few more covered minutes if needed.

name: Veg Biryani

ingredients.prep: thinly sliced (half for fried onions, half for the masala)
pounded to a paste with the garlic
pounded to a paste with the ginger

ingredients.item: shahi jeera (black cumin, not kalonji/nigella) or cumin seeds

steps: Rinse the basmati rice until the water runs clear, soak it for 30 minutes, then drain. If using saffron, soak it in the warm milk now.

Heat the oil in a heavy-bottomed pot on medium heat and fry half the onion, stirring often, for 10-12 minutes until deep golden brown and crisp. Lift the fried onions out onto a plate, leaving the oil in the pot.

In the same oil, fry the rest of the onion for 5-6 minutes until golden. Add the ginger-garlic paste and green chilli and saute for 1 minute, then add the tomato and cook for 4-5 minutes until soft and mushy.
Add the turmeric powder, red chilli powder and biryani masala and stir for 30 seconds. Add the potato, cauliflower, carrot, french beans and peas and stir for 2 minutes to coat them in the masala.

Turn the heat to low, stir in the whisked curd and salt, stirring continuously for a minute so the curd does not split. Add half the mint and coriander, cover and cook on low-medium for 8-10 minutes until the vegetables are about three-quarters cooked and the masala is thick and clinging, not watery. Add a splash of water only if it starts to stick.

Meanwhile, bring the water to a rolling boil in a large pan with the bay leaf, cinnamon, cloves, cardamom, shahi jeera and enough salt that the water tastes clearly salty. Add the drained rice and boil uncovered for 5-6 minutes until the grains have lengthened and a pressed grain breaks with a firm white core (about 70-75 percent cooked). Drain at once.

Spread the vegetable masala in an even layer at the bottom of the pot. Spoon the drained rice over it loosely without pressing. Top with the fried onions, the remaining mint and coriander, the saffron milk (if using), the ghee and the lemon juice.

Cover with a tight lid (seal the rim with foil or a rope of dough if it is loose). Cook on medium for 3 minutes until steam builds, then set the pot on a hot tawa over the lowest heat and cook for 20 minutes.
Switch off the heat and rest the biryani covered for 10 minutes. Open, and serve by scooping gently from the side down to the bottom so every portion has rice and vegetables.
tips: Drain the rice when it is only about 70-75 percent cooked; it finishes in the steam, and fully boiled rice turns mushy during dum.
Keep the masala thick but moist before layering; a watery masala makes the bottom rice soggy, a dry one scorches.
The tawa under the pot during dum spreads the heat so the bottom layer does not burn.

name: Veg Clear Soup
servesWith: as a starter before Veg Fried Rice or Hakka Noodles

ingredients.prep: chopped, whites and greens kept separate

steps: Finely chop the carrot, beans, cabbage and celery into small, even pieces about the size of a pea. Finely chop the garlic and ginger, and keep the spring onion whites and greens separate.
Heat the oil in a pot on medium-high heat. Add the garlic, ginger and celery and saute for 30-40 seconds until fragrant, without letting the garlic brown.
Add the spring onion whites, carrot and beans and stir-fry on high heat for 1-2 minutes.
Add the cabbage, toss for 30 seconds, then pour in the water or stock. Bring to a boil, then simmer on medium heat for 5-6 minutes, until the vegetables are just tender but still have a bite.
Add the salt, pepper, soy sauce and the vinegar if using, and simmer for 1 more minute. Taste and adjust the seasoning.
Turn off the heat, stir in the spring onion greens and serve piping hot.
tips: Use only a little soy sauce, just to season; the broth should stay pale and clear.
Do not add cornflour; that turns it into a thick soup rather than a clear one.
Do not overboil; the vegetables should stay crunchy and brightly coloured.

name: Veg Cutlet
servesWith: tomato ketchup or green chutney with tea

ingredients.prep: peeled and very finely chopped or grated

ingredients.item: bread crumbs (for the mixture and coating)

steps: Pressure cook the whole, unpeeled potatoes with about a cup of water for 3 whistles on medium heat (or boil until a knife slides in). Peel, mash while warm and set aside to cool.
Heat the oil for sauteing in a pan on medium heat. Add the onion and saute 2 minutes until soft, then add the ginger, garlic and green chilli and stir for 30 seconds until fragrant.

Add the carrot, beans, peas and salt and sprinkle in a little water, just enough to make steam. Cover and cook on low heat for 8-10 minutes, stirring now and then, until the vegetables are tender and the peas crush easily. Uncover and cook 1-2 minutes more until no moisture is left in the pan.
Stir in the turmeric powder, red chilli powder, garam masala and chaat masala and cook for 1 minute. Take off the heat and let it cool.

Combine the cooked vegetables with the mashed potato, coriander leaves and a little of the bread crumbs. Knead into a mixture that holds its shape without sticking; add more bread crumbs a spoon at a time if it feels soft.
Divide into equal portions and shape into oval or round patties about half an inch thick.

Whisk the cornflour with a little water into a thin, smooth slurry. Dip each cutlet in the slurry, then roll it in the remaining bread crumbs to coat evenly. Refrigerate for 15 minutes so the coating sets.
Heat the oil for shallow frying in a flat pan on medium heat. Fry the cutlets 3-4 minutes per side until golden brown and crisp. Drain on paper and serve hot.
tips: Chop the vegetables very fine and cook them until dry - wet vegetables are the main reason cutlets break in the pan.
Chilling the coated cutlets for 15 minutes keeps the crumb coat from falling off while frying.
Fry on medium heat; on high the crust browns before the inside is heated through.

name: Veg Fried Rice

ingredients.prep: finely chopped into small even pieces
chopped, whites and greens kept separate

steps: Rinse the basmati rice in 2-3 changes of water and soak it for 20 minutes. Boil it in a large pot of salted water on high heat for 6-8 minutes, checking from 5, until a grain pressed between your fingers is just cooked through but still firm and whole, with a slight bite; it finishes cooking in the wok. Drain well.

Spread the drained rice on a wide plate and let it cool completely, at least 30 minutes, or refrigerate it. Chilled leftover rice from the previous day works even better; with it, skip both the boiling and this cooling.

While the rice cools, finely chop the carrot, beans, capsicum, garlic and green chilli, finely shred the cabbage, and keep the spring onion whites and greens separate. Keep everything beside the stove, because the stir-fry moves fast.

Heat the oil in a wok or wide kadai on high heat until it shimmers. Add the garlic, green chilli and spring onion whites and stir for 20-30 seconds, until the garlic smells fragrant but has not browned.
Add the carrot and beans and stir-fry on high heat for about 2 minutes. Add the cabbage and capsicum and toss for 1 minute more; the vegetables should be hot and bright but still crunchy.

Add the cooled rice, breaking up any lumps with your fingers as it goes in. Sprinkle over the pepper and a little salt, and pour the soy sauce and vinegar around the hot sides of the wok rather than straight onto the rice.
Toss on high heat for 2-3 minutes, lifting and turning the rice rather than pressing it, until every grain is evenly coloured and steaming hot.
Turn off the heat, mix in the spring onion greens, taste and adjust the salt, and serve hot.
tips: Use completely cold rice; freshly cooked, warm rice turns sticky and mushy in the wok. With cold leftover rice you skip the soaking, boiling and cooling, and the dish takes about 20 minutes.
Keep the flame on high throughout and do not crowd the wok; for more than 3 servings, fry the rice in two batches.
Soy sauce is already salty, so add salt sparingly and taste only after the soy sauce has gone in.

name: Veg Hakka Noodles

ingredients.prep: chopped, whites and greens kept separate

steps: Bring a large pot of water to a rolling boil with a little salt. Add the noodles and cook for the time on the packet, usually 3-4 minutes, stirring once to separate them, until just tender with a slight bite.
Drain, rinse under cold running water until cool, drain thoroughly and toss with a few drops of the oil so the strands do not stick. Leave them in the colander to dry while you chop.
Thinly slice the onion and capsicum, cut the carrot into matchsticks, finely shred the cabbage, finely chop the garlic, slit the green chilli, and keep the spring onion whites and greens separate.

Heat the remaining oil in a wok on high heat until it shimmers. Add the garlic and green chilli and stir for 20 seconds, then add the onion and spring onion whites and toss for about 1 minute, until the onion edges turn translucent.
Add the carrot, then the cabbage and capsicum, and stir-fry on high heat for about 2 minutes; the vegetables should soften slightly at the edges but stay crunchy.

Add the noodles, then the salt, pepper, soy sauce, vinegar and chilli sauce if using. Toss with tongs or two spatulas, lifting from the bottom, for about 2 minutes until the noodles are evenly coated and hot.
Turn off the heat, toss in the spring onion greens and serve immediately.
tips: Boil the noodles until just tender, never soft; they cook further in the wok and overboiled noodles break and clump.
Rinse and oil the noodles and let them drain dry, so they toss loose instead of steaming into a lump.
Toss with tongs or two forks instead of stirring with a spoon, which snaps the strands.

name: Veg Pulao
steps: Rinse the basmati rice in 3-4 changes of water until the water runs almost clear, soak it in fresh water for 20-30 minutes, then drain it well in a sieve.
Heat the oil in a heavy-bottomed pot on medium heat. Add the cumin seeds, bay leaf, cinnamon, cloves and cardamom and let them sizzle for about 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add the onion and green chilli and fry, stirring, for 4-5 minutes until the onion turns light golden.
Add the ginger and garlic and saute for 1 minute until the raw smell goes.
Add the carrot, french beans, cauliflower and peas and stir-fry for 2-3 minutes on medium heat.
Pour in the water, add salt and bring it to a rolling boil on high heat. Taste the water: it should be a little saltier than you would like a soup.
Add the drained rice and stir gently once. Let it boil uncovered for 3-4 minutes until the water drops to the level of the rice and small holes appear on the surface.
Turn the heat to the lowest setting, cover with a tight-fitting lid and cook for 12-15 minutes without opening or stirring.
Switch off the heat and leave it covered for 10 minutes. Fluff gently with a fork, then scatter the coriander leaves, and the mint leaves if using, over the top.
tips: Do not stir once the lid is on; stirring breaks the soaked grains and makes the pulao sticky.
In a pressure cooker, use 1.5 times the rice's volume of water, cook for 1 whistle on medium and let the pressure drop on its own before opening.
The 10-minute rest is what firms the grains so they separate when fluffed; skipping it gives wet, clumpy rice.

name: Mixed Vegetable Sambar
servesWith: hot rice, or idli and dosa

ingredients.prep: cut into 1-inch cubes, kept in water until used
cut into large chunks; small onions peeled and left whole

steps: Rinse the toor dal twice, then pressure-cook it with the turmeric powder and three times its volume of water for 4-5 whistles on medium, until it mashes completely under a spoon. Whisk it smooth.
Soak the tamarind in hot water - about 1/4 cup per serving - for 10 minutes, squeeze it well and strain the pulp, discarding the fibre and seeds.

Heat the oil in a heavy pot on medium. Add the mustard seeds and let them splutter, then add the fenugreek seeds and fry for 15-20 seconds until light golden - not dark, or the sambar turns bitter. Add the dried red chilli, curry leaves and asafoetida and stir for 5-10 seconds.

Add the onion and green chilli and saute for 2-3 minutes, until chopped onion turns translucent (whole small onions only need to turn glossy and soften at the edges - they finish cooking in the sambar). Add the tomato and cook 2-3 minutes until soft.

Add the drumstick (if using, cut into 3-inch pieces), carrot and beans and stir for a minute. Pour in the tamarind water, add the sambar powder, salt and enough water to cover the vegetables by an inch. Cover and boil on medium for 5 minutes.
Add the drained brinjal, cover and cook another 6-8 minutes, until every vegetable is tender when pierced with a knife and the raw smell of tamarind has gone.

Stir in the mashed dal (and the jaggery, if using). Add hot water to bring it to a medium-thick, pourable consistency and simmer on low for 5 minutes, until it froths up and the dal and tamarind come together. Do not boil it hard.
Switch off, stir in the coriander leaves, and let the sambar rest covered for 10 minutes before serving.
tips: Cook the dal completely soft before it meets the tamarind - acid stops dal from softening any further, so undercooked dal stays grainy in the sambar.
Sambar thickens as it stands; leave it slightly thinner than you want it at the table.
Store-bought sambar powders vary a lot in heat - add a little less, taste after the vegetables cook, and add more then.

name: Vendakkai Mor Kuzhambu
servesWith: hot rice with a poriyal on the side

ingredients.prep: washed, dried completely, cut into 1-inch pieces

steps: Soak the toor dal and chana dal together in warm water for 30 minutes.
Wash the okra and pat every piece completely dry before cutting; trim the ends and cut into 1-inch pieces.
Drain the dals and grind them with the grated coconut, green chilli, ginger, cumin seeds and coriander seeds (if using) to a very smooth paste, adding a little water.
Whisk the sour curd with the turmeric powder, salt and 2-3 tablespoons of water per serving until completely smooth and lump-free - it should pour like thick buttermilk, not sit like curd.

Heat two-thirds of the coconut oil in a kadai on medium. Add the okra with a pinch of salt and fry uncovered for 6-8 minutes, stirring occasionally, until tender, lightly browned at the edges and no longer sticky.
Add the ground paste and a little water (about 1/4 cup for 2 servings) to the okra and simmer on low-medium for 3-4 minutes, stirring, until it thickens and the raw smell of the dal is gone.
Turn the heat to its lowest, pour in the whisked curd and stir continuously for 2-3 minutes, until it is hot and just begins to froth at the edges. Switch off before it boils.
In a small pan, heat the remaining coconut oil on medium, splutter the mustard seeds, then add the dried red chilli, curry leaves and asafoetida for 10 seconds. Pour over the kuzhambu and serve.
tips: Never let it boil once the curd is in - it splits into grainy curds and whey.
Use sour, day-old curd; fresh curd tastes flat in mor kuzhambu.
Dry the okra before cutting and fry it until the slime is gone, or the kuzhambu turns stringy.

name: Zucchini Stir-fry
servesWith: pasta, garlic bread or a bowl of soup

ingredients.prep: halved lengthwise, cut into half-moons about 1/2 cm thick

steps: Wash the zucchini and trim both ends; there is no need to peel it. Halve it lengthwise and cut into half-moons about 1/2 cm thick. Finely chop the garlic.
Heat the oil in a wide pan on medium-high heat until hot. Add the zucchini in a single layer and leave it undisturbed for about 2 minutes, until the undersides are lightly browned.
Toss and cook for 2-3 minutes more, stirring now and then, until the zucchini is tender-crisp; it should bend slightly but not be soft or watery.
Push the zucchini to the sides, add the garlic and chilli flakes to the cleared centre and stir for 30-45 seconds until fragrant, then toss everything together.
Turn off the heat. Season with salt, pepper and the oregano if using, toss, and squeeze over the lemon juice if using. Serve immediately.
tips: Salt only at the end; salting early draws water out and the zucchini stews instead of browning.
Use a wide pan and do not crowd it; cook in two batches if the slices overlap.
Take it off the heat while still slightly firm, as it keeps softening on the plate.
